questions.practicalNote: Many governments run declassification reviews and train staff to classify at the lowest level that fits.

questions.stem: A confidential pricing spreadsheet is regularly emailed to a distributor, who saves and forwards it inside their own company. Which control BEST ensures the recipients can still tell it is confidential?
options: Folder permissions on the share where the original copy is kept
A DLP rule that blocks the file if it is sent to a webmail domain
A visible confidential marking in the header and footer of the file
TLS encryption of the email connection used to send the file
rationales: Folder permissions protect the original copy only; they mean nothing once the file has been sent.
DLP controls the sender's outbound mail; it does not tell recipients how to treat the file.
Correct. A marking on the document itself travels with every copy and tells each reader how to handle it.
TLS protects the file in transit only; after delivery it carries no indication of sensitivity.
questions.concept: Marking travels with the information; system controls stay behind.
questions.trap: Choosing a technical control that only works inside your own systems.
questions.managerLens: When data leaves your control, make sure its classification leaves with it.
questions.practicalNote: Labelling tools can add both a visible marking and embedded metadata at the same time.
questions.gap: Knowing what marking and labelling achieve.

questions.stem: Each week a bank sends backup tapes holding customer data to an offsite vault by courier. A tape went missing last year and was never found. What MOST reduces the impact of a tape being lost in transit?
options: Using a bonded courier with tracked vehicles and vetted drivers
Encrypting the tapes, with the keys managed separately at the bank
Sealing the tapes in tamper-evident bags before collection
Logging a chain-of-custody signature at every handover point
rationales: A better courier lowers the chance of loss but does nothing for the data on a tape that still goes missing.
Correct. Encryption with separately held keys means a lost tape exposes nothing, which reduces impact rather than just likelihood.
Tamper-evident bags show whether a tape was opened; they do not protect the data on a lost tape.
Chain of custody shows where a tape was lost; it does not protect its contents.
questions.concept: Encrypt media in transit; other controls reduce likelihood or aid detection.
questions.trap: Picking the control that sounds most like transport security.
questions.managerLens: Ask what happens when the control fails; encryption still protects the data when the tape is lost.
questions.practicalNote: LTO tape drives support hardware encryption, with keys held in a key manager rather than on the tape.
questions.gap: Distinguishing impact reduction from likelihood reduction.

questions.stem: A company is writing handling requirements for paper documents classified RESTRICTED. Which TWO belong in those requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Storage in locked cabinets when the documents are not in use
Destruction with a cross-cut shredder at the end of their life
The data owner's choice of which documents are RESTRICTED
Board approval of the company's classification scheme
The asset tag of each printer used to print the documents
rationales: Correct. How documents must be stored is a core handling requirement.
Correct. How documents must be destroyed is a core handling requirement.
Deciding the classification happens before handling; handling rules apply once it is set.
Approving the scheme is governance of the scheme, not a handling rule.
Printer asset tags are inventory detail, not handling rules for documents.
questions.concept: Handling requirements cover storage, transmission, sharing and destruction for each class.
questions.trap: Mixing classification decisions or governance into handling rules.
questions.managerLens: Write handling rules per class so staff know exactly what to do with each label.
questions.practicalNote: A one-page handling matrix per classification level is easier for staff than a long policy.

questions.stem: A newly appointed security manager at a manufacturing firm wants to build an asset protection programme. What must the firm have BEFORE it can protect its assets well?
options: A classification label on each document it produces
Encryption on each laptop and server in the company
A configuration baseline for each type of server it runs
An accurate inventory of its hardware, software and data
rationales: Labelling documents needs a classification scheme and knowledge of what data exists first.
Encryption is one control; deciding where it is needed depends on knowing what assets exist.
Baselines apply to known systems; unknown systems will be missed.
Correct. You cannot protect, classify or monitor what you do not know you have. The inventory comes first.
questions.concept: An asset inventory is the foundation of asset security.
questions.trap: Jumping to a control before knowing what exists.
questions.managerLens: Fund the inventory and keep it current; every other control depends on it.
questions.practicalNote: Inventories are usually built from discovery scans, CMDB records, procurement data and cloud account listings.
questions.gap: Seeing the inventory as the starting point.

questions.stem: A marketing team has paid for a SaaS CRM on a corporate credit card for a year. It holds 40,000 customer records, and IT has just found out about it through expense reports. What should happen FIRST?
options: Add it to the asset inventory and assign an owner accountable for it
Block the service's domain at the web proxy until a review is done
Migrate its records into the corporate CRM and close the account
Run a penetration test of the SaaS application to check its security
rationales: Correct. First make the asset known and owned. Only then can its data, contract and risks be assessed and a decision made.
Blocking straight away disrupts a working business process and may cut off access to customer data without knowing the risk.
Migration may be the end state, but deciding it before understanding the data and contract is premature.
Testing a provider's system without its permission is likely to breach its terms and may be illegal.
questions.concept: Bring shadow IT under management: inventory and ownership first.
questions.trap: Reacting with a technical block or test before understanding the asset.
questions.managerLens: Make the business accountable, then assess, then decide.
questions.practicalNote: CASB discovery and expense reviews are common ways to find unsanctioned SaaS.

questions.stem: A company is extending its asset inventory beyond hardware. Which TWO of the following are intangible assets the inventory should include? (Select TWO.)
options: Software licences the company has bought
Internet domain names the company has registered
Laptops issued to the sales team
Racks in the company's server room
Backup tapes stored at the offsite vault
rationales: Correct. Licences are intangible assets with value and compliance obligations.
Correct. Domain names are intangible assets; losing one can take services offline and enable impersonation.
Laptops are physical hardware, so they are tangible assets.
Server racks are physical equipment, so they are tangible assets.
Tapes are tangible media, although the data on them is an intangible asset.
questions.concept: Inventories include intangible assets: data, software, licences, domain names, intellectual property.
questions.trap: Thinking of assets as hardware only.
questions.managerLens: Track the assets whose loss would hurt, whatever their form.
questions.practicalNote: Expired domain registrations have caused outages and phishing risk; give domains an owner and renewal alerts.

questions.stem: Law requires a bank to keep transaction records for seven years. The marketing team wants to keep customers' app-browsing data indefinitely 'in case it is useful for analytics'. What is the BEST approach?
options: Keep everything indefinitely, since storage is cheap and data may prove useful
Keep everything for seven years to match the longest legal requirement
Set retention for each record type from its legal and business need, then delete on schedule
Let each department decide how long to keep the data it collects
rationales: Indefinite retention increases breach impact and conflicts with privacy rules that limit keeping personal data longer than needed.
Applying the longest period to everything keeps browsing data far longer than any need justifies.
Correct. Retention should be set per type of record from the legal requirement and the genuine business purpose, then enforced by deletion.
Department-by-department decisions lead to inconsistency and over-retention; retention needs a governed schedule.
questions.concept: Retention schedules are set per record type and enforced by deletion.
questions.trap: Treating retention as one number for everything, or as 'keep it just in case'.
questions.managerLens: Data you keep is data you must protect; keep only what you need for as long as you need it.
questions.practicalNote: Retention schedules usually sit with records management and legal, and are enforced through automated deletion.

questions.stem: A retailer's loyalty app records each customer's exact GPS location every minute. The only business use is to show offers for the customer's city. What should the retailer change?
options: Encrypt the GPS records at rest and carry on collecting them
Collect only the customer's city, as that is all the purpose needs
Ask customers to consent to continuous location tracking in the app
Delete the GPS records after twelve months instead of keeping them
rationales: Encryption protects the data but does not justify collecting far more than the purpose needs.
Correct. Data minimisation: collect only what the purpose requires. City-level location meets the need with far less risk.
Consent does not make excessive collection necessary, and many laws still require minimisation.
Shorter retention helps, but collecting precise location every minute is still unnecessary.
questions.concept: Data minimisation: collect only what the purpose needs.
questions.trap: Adding a control or consent to data that should not be collected at all.
questions.managerLens: The cheapest data to protect is data you never collected.
questions.practicalNote: Privacy laws including GDPR and Zimbabwe's data protection act include minimisation and purpose limitation principles.

questions.stem: A company is ending its IaaS contract and moving to another provider. It has no access to the provider's physical disks, which are shared with other tenants. Which TWO measures BEST address data remanence? (Select TWO.)
options: Encrypt data with company-held keys from the start, then destroy the keys at exit
Obtain contractual commitments and evidence of the provider's media sanitisation
Overwrite the volumes three times with random data before closing the account
Ask the provider to hand over the physical disks used by the company's account
Delete the virtual machines and storage accounts before the contract ends
rationales: Correct. If the data was encrypted with keys only the company controls, destroying the keys makes any remnants unreadable: cryptographic erase.
Correct. The provider sanitises the physical media; contract terms and evidence such as audit reports are how the customer gets assurance.
Overwriting virtual volumes may not touch the physical blocks that held the data, because storage is virtualised and spread.
Disks are shared between tenants and providers will not hand them over; it is not a practical measure.
Deleting resources removes access, but data can remain on the underlying media.
questions.concept: In the cloud, remanence is handled by customer-held encryption keys and the provider's assured sanitisation.
questions.trap: Applying on-premises techniques that do not reach the physical media.
questions.managerLens: Plan exit at entry: customer-managed keys and sanitisation terms belong in the original contract.
questions.practicalNote: Major providers describe their media sanitisation in their SOC 2 reports and security documentation.
questions.gap: Handling remanence where you do not control the hardware.

questions.subtopic: End of life and end of support
questions.stem: A vendor announces end of life for a firewall model the company relies on. It will stop selling the model this year but will issue security updates for three more years. What does this mean for the company?
options: It must replace the firewalls now, since they are no longer secure
Security updates stop immediately, so the firewalls must be isolated
It should buy spare units now and plan to run them for as long as possible
It can keep using them securely but should plan replacement before support ends
rationales: End of sale does not make the product insecure while updates continue.
Updates continue for three years; this confuses end of life with end of support.
Stockpiling to run past end of support leaves the company on unpatched firewalls later.
Correct. End of life is a planning signal: the firewalls stay supportable for three years, and replacement should be budgeted and scheduled before updates stop.
questions.concept: End of life (no longer sold) is not end of support (no more updates).
questions.trap: Treating end of life as immediate insecurity, or planning to run past end of support.
questions.managerLens: Use the support window to budget and plan an orderly replacement.
questions.practicalNote: Track EOL and EOS dates in the asset inventory so replacements reach the budget cycle in time.

questions.stem: An email server is scheduled for disposal under the retention schedule this month. Legal has placed a litigation hold on the mailboxes of three former directors that are stored on it. What should happen?
options: Preserve the held mailboxes as legal directs; dispose of the server once they are secured or released
Sanitise the server on schedule, since the disposal date is set in approved policy
Copy the three mailboxes to a USB drive and give it to the legal department
Go ahead with disposal if the server's disks are encrypted, since the data is safe
rationales: Correct. A legal hold overrides normal retention and disposal. The data must be preserved in a forensically sound way agreed with legal before the hardware is disposed of.
Destroying data under a legal hold can be spoliation of evidence, with serious legal consequences, whatever the schedule says.
An ad hoc copy on a USB drive may not preserve integrity or metadata and creates a new unprotected copy.
Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not preserve the evidence the hold requires.
questions.concept: Legal holds override retention and disposal schedules.
questions.trap: Following the schedule mechanically, or preserving data in an unsound way.
questions.managerLens: Make legal hold checks a mandatory step before any disposal.
questions.practicalNote: e-Discovery tools can place mailboxes on hold and export them with metadata intact.
questions.gap: Knowing how legal holds interact with retention and disposal.

questions.stem: A finance officer's laptop is being retired after five years. Which TWO steps belong in its retirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Sanitise its storage to a level that fits the data it held
Record its disposal in the asset inventory with the date
Remove its asset tag so that it can no longer be traced
Note the user's password in the file for future audits
Hand it to a new joiner straight away without changes
rationales: Correct. The storage must be sanitised according to its classification before the device leaves.
Correct. The inventory must show the asset's disposal, keeping the record accurate for audits.
Traceability should be kept through disposal, not removed.
Recording passwords is a security failure, not an audit control.
Reissuing a device with a previous user's data on it exposes that data.
questions.concept: Retirement: sanitise, record and dispose of assets in a controlled way.
questions.trap: Thinking retirement is just switching the device off.
questions.managerLens: Make disposal a recorded process with evidence, not an ad hoc task.
questions.practicalNote: Disposal vendors should issue certificates of sanitisation per serial number.
questions.gap: Knowing the steps of asset retirement.

questions.stem: A payment application encrypts its database and uses TLS for every connection. An attacker who gains access to the application server's memory can still read card numbers. Which data state is unprotected?
options: Data at rest
Data in transit
Data in use
Data in archive
rationales: The database is encrypted, so stored data is protected.
TLS protects data moving across the network.
Correct. Data being processed sits decrypted in memory; protecting it needs controls such as access restriction, secure enclaves or tokenisation.
Archive is a form of storage at rest, which is encrypted here.
questions.concept: Data has three states; data in use is the hardest to protect.
questions.trap: Assuming encryption at rest and in transit covers everything.
questions.managerLens: Ask how data is protected in every state, including while it is processed.
questions.practicalNote: Confidential computing (hardware enclaves) and memory scraping defences address data in use.

questions.stem: A company adopts the NIST SP 800-53 moderate baseline. It first removes the wireless controls because it runs no wireless networks. It then changes the account lockout threshold in the baseline to fit its help desk process. What are these two steps?
options: Tailoring, then scoping
Scoping, then tailoring
Scoping both times
Tailoring both times
rationales: The order is reversed: removing controls that do not apply comes first.
Correct. Removing controls that do not apply is scoping; adjusting a remaining control's parameters is tailoring.
Changing a parameter of a control that still applies is not scoping.
Dropping controls for technology that is not present is scoping, not tailoring.
questions.concept: Scoping chooses which controls apply; tailoring adjusts them.
questions.trap: Using the two terms interchangeably.
questions.managerLens: Document both decisions and their reasons so auditors can follow them.
questions.practicalNote: SP 800-53B baselines are designed to be tailored; overlays package common tailoring decisions.

questions.stem: Staff at a consultancy upload client lists to personal cloud storage accounts. Separately, sensitive client reports are being forwarded to competitors by staff who have since left. Which TWO controls address these problems MOST directly? (Select TWO.)
options: A CASB that controls uploads to unsanctioned cloud services
DRM so protected reports cannot be opened once access is revoked
Full-disk encryption on all the consultancy's staff laptops
A web application firewall in front of the client portal
Longer and more complex passwords for staff accounts
rationales: Correct. A CASB gives visibility of cloud use and can block uploads to unsanctioned services.
Correct. DRM keeps control with the file itself, so access can be withdrawn even after a copy has left.
Disk encryption protects lost laptops, not deliberate uploads or forwarding.
A WAF protects a web application from attacks, not data being taken by insiders.
Password strength does not stop authorised users moving data.
questions.concept: CASB governs cloud use; DRM controls use of files after they leave.
questions.trap: Choosing a strong general control that does not address data movement.
questions.managerLens: Match each data protection tool to the path the data takes out.
questions.practicalNote: Rights management in office suites can revoke access to sensitive files when someone leaves.
questions.gap: Knowing what DLP, CASB and DRM each do.

questions.stem: An online travel agent must meet PCI DSS for card payments and GDPR for its European customers, and it runs an ISO/IEC 27001 management system. Its small team is overwhelmed by separate compliance efforts. What is the BEST approach?
options: Run three separate compliance programmes, each with its own owner
Implement PCI DSS only, as it is the most prescriptive of the three
Focus on whichever standard the next external audit will test
Build one control set mapped to each requirement and evidence it once
rationales: Separate programmes duplicate effort and produce inconsistent controls.
PCI DSS covers card data only; it does not meet GDPR or the wider ISMS.
Chasing the next audit leaves the other obligations unmet and creates last-minute work.
Correct. A unified control framework mapped to each obligation lets one control satisfy several requirements, with one set of evidence.
questions.concept: Select and map standards so one control set meets every applicable requirement.
questions.trap: Treating each obligation as a separate project, or picking one and ignoring the rest.
questions.managerLens: Design once, comply many times: map controls to every obligation.
questions.practicalNote: ISO 27001's Statement of Applicability is a natural place to map controls to PCI DSS and GDPR requirements.

questions.stem: A merchant wants to take card numbers out of most of its systems to reduce PCI DSS scope, while still being able to process refunds and repeat purchases. Which method BEST achieves this?
options: Tokenisation, with card numbers held in a separate secured vault
Encrypting card numbers in each system, with keys kept on those systems
Hashing card numbers so that they cannot be read in the databases
Masking all but the last four digits wherever card numbers are shown
rationales: Correct. Systems hold tokens with no exploitable value; card numbers live only in the vault, and refunds use the token. This is what reduces scope.
Systems that hold encrypted card numbers and can reach the keys stay in scope.
A hash cannot be turned back into a card number, so refunds and repeat charges would fail.
Masking changes what is displayed, but the full number is still stored, so systems stay in scope.
questions.concept: Tokenisation removes sensitive values from systems; encryption protects them in place.
questions.trap: Choosing encryption because it sounds strongest.
questions.managerLens: Reducing where sensitive data lives is often cheaper than protecting it everywhere.
questions.practicalNote: Many payment gateways offer tokenisation so merchants never store card numbers at all.
questions.gap: Distinguishing tokenisation, encryption, hashing and masking.

questions.stem: A defence contractor's system must stop a process running at Secret from writing data to an Unclassified file, yet it allows the same process to append entries to a Top Secret audit log. Which rule is being enforced?
options: The Biba integrity star property
The Bell-LaPadula star property
The Bell-LaPadula simple security property
The Clark-Wilson separation of duty rule
rationales: Biba's star property protects integrity: no write up. It would block the append to the higher level, which this system allows.
Correct. Bell-LaPadula's star property (no write down) stops a subject leaking data to a lower classification, while writing up is permitted.
The simple security property governs reading (no read up). The scenario is about writing.
Clark-Wilson enforces integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties. It does not use classification levels.
questions.concept: Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality: no read up, no write down.
questions.trap: Mixing up Biba (integrity) and Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality), which both have a star property.
questions.managerLens: Model choice follows the protection goal; confidentiality-first environments such as defence use Bell-LaPadula-style rules.
questions.practicalNote: Mandatory access control systems such as SELinux in MLS mode enforce these rules with labels.
questions.gap: Not linking each model to its security goal and its read and write rules.

questions.stem: A foreign ministry must keep diplomatic cables confidential for at least 25 years. Traffic between embassies runs over TLS 1.3 using ECDHE key exchange and AES-256-GCM. An adversary is known to record the ministry's internet traffic in bulk. Which threat to these cables is MOST significant over that period?
options: Grover's algorithm reducing AES-256 to an insecure effective key length
Certificate expiry causing outages between embassy and ministry systems
Collision attacks against the SHA-256 hashes used in the TLS handshakes
Captured sessions decrypted later, once quantum computers break ECDHE
rationales: Grover's algorithm roughly halves the effective strength of a symmetric key, leaving AES-256 at about 128-bit security, which is still considered adequate.
An availability problem worth managing, but it does not expose the content of the cables.
No practical SHA-256 collision attack exists, and a collision would not reveal the contents of past sessions.

Correct. This is 'harvest now, decrypt later'. A large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break elliptic-curve key exchange and expose the session keys of recorded traffic. Data that must stay secret for decades is the first priority for post-quantum key exchange such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203).
questions.concept: Harvest now, decrypt later: long confidentiality lifetimes drive early migration to post-quantum key exchange.
questions.trap: Worrying about symmetric ciphers, which quantum computing weakens only modestly, instead of public-key exchange.
questions.managerLens: Prioritise post-quantum migration by data lifetime: anything that must stay secret beyond the expected arrival of quantum attacks goes first.
questions.practicalNote: Hybrid key exchange (classical X25519 combined with ML-KEM) is already enabled by default in major browsers and TLS libraries.
questions.gap: Not knowing which algorithms quantum computing actually breaks.

questions.stem: Gwayi's CFO assumes that moving the ERP system to the IaaS provider makes the provider responsible for its security. Which responsibility stays with Gwayi under the IaaS model?
options: Physical security of the provider's data centres and their access control
Patching the hypervisors that host Gwayi's virtual machines
Replacing failed disks in the provider's storage arrays
Hardening and patching the operating systems of Gwayi's virtual machines
rationales: Physical security of the facilities is the provider's responsibility in every cloud model.
The hypervisor layer belongs to the provider in IaaS.
Underlying hardware, including storage, is the provider's to maintain.
Correct. In IaaS the customer manages everything from the guest operating system up: OS hardening and patching, applications, data, identities and network rules inside its virtual network.
questions.concept: Shared responsibility: in IaaS the customer secures the guest OS and everything above it.
questions.trap: Believing that moving to the cloud moves all security to the provider.
questions.managerLens: Write down the split for each service model and check the provider's attestations cover their share.
questions.practicalNote: Most cloud breaches come from the customer's share: misconfigured storage, weak identities, unpatched VMs.
questions.gap: Knowing what each cloud model leaves to the customer.

questions.stem: The plant's PLCs cannot be patched, and engineers want to monitor the SCADA historian from head office. Which TWO measures BEST manage the risk? (Select TWO.)
options: Keep the OT network segmented from the corporate network, with tightly filtered flows
Allow head office access only through a monitored jump host or one-way data diode
Install the corporate antivirus agent on the PLCs and the SCADA historian
Join the PLCs and historian to the corporate Active Directory domain
Run weekly authenticated vulnerability scans across the PLC network
rationales: Correct. Segmentation limits who and what can reach unpatchable controllers.
Correct. A controlled, monitored path (or one-way transfer of historian data) gives engineers visibility without exposing control systems.
PLCs cannot run general-purpose antivirus, and unapproved software on control systems can affect safety and vendor support.
Domain-joining OT assets ties them to IT's attack surface; a compromised domain would reach the plant.
Active scanning can disrupt fragile PLCs and stop production; OT usually relies on passive monitoring.
questions.concept: Unpatchable OT is protected by isolation, controlled access paths and passive monitoring.
questions.trap: Applying IT practices such as AV, domain joins and active scans to control systems.
questions.managerLens: In OT, safety and availability come first; prefer controls that cannot stop the plant.
questions.practicalNote: IEC 62443 zones and conduits and the Purdue model are common ways to structure OT segmentation.

questions.stem: Gwayi is choosing fire suppression for the new head office server room, where two engineers work most of the day. Water damage to equipment is a concern, but staff safety is the priority. Which option BEST fits?
options: A clean agent system designed to be safe for occupied spaces
Total-flooding carbon dioxide for fast extinguishing
A wet-pipe sprinkler system charged with water at all times
A new Halon 1301 system, which is highly effective on electrical fires
rationales: Correct. Clean agents such as FK-5-1-12 or FM-200 extinguish without water damage and are designed to be safe for people at their design concentration.
CO2 at extinguishing concentrations is lethal; it suits unoccupied spaces only.
Wet pipes can discharge from a damaged head and soak equipment; pre-action would be safer than wet pipe if water is used.
Halon production was banned under the Montreal Protocol; new Halon systems are not installed.
questions.concept: Choose suppression to protect people first, then equipment.
questions.trap: Choosing the most effective extinguisher without considering occupants.
questions.managerLens: Life safety is non-negotiable; within that, minimise damage to assets.
questions.practicalNote: Clean agent rooms need sealed walls, door fans tests and abort switches; local fire codes also apply.
questions.gap: Matching suppression systems to occupied spaces.

questions.stem: A payments API sends every request to a central authorisation service to check the caller's permissions. During a network fault, the API cannot reach that service for several minutes. How should the API behave?
options: Allow requests from callers whose permissions it has checked in the last hour
Deny the requests and raise an alert until the service is back
Allow every request, so that customers are not affected by the outage
Queue the requests and approve them automatically when the service returns
rationales: Stale decisions may allow callers whose access has since been revoked; it is a fail-open shortcut.
Correct. Failing securely means denying access when the control cannot make a decision, and alerting so the fault is fixed.
Allowing everything turns an outage into an open door; attackers can even cause outages for this reason.
Automatic approval later still processes requests nobody authorised.
questions.concept: Fail securely: when a security control cannot decide, deny.
questions.trap: Putting availability ahead of authorisation for financial transactions.
questions.managerLens: Decide failure behaviour at design time and get the business owner to accept the availability impact.
questions.practicalNote: Short-lived cached decisions with strict expiry are sometimes accepted, but only as a documented, risk-assessed design.

questions.stem: A design review of a new mobile banking back end proposes several changes. Which THREE apply recognised secure design principles? (Select THREE.)
options: Give each service account just the permissions its service needs
Validate input in the application as well as at the web application firewall
Require two administrators to approve export of production signing keys
Open all firewall ports during deployments and close them afterwards
Show detailed stack traces in production error messages to speed up support
Let the operations team share one administrator account for simplicity
rationales: Correct. Least privilege limits what a compromised service account can do.
Correct. Defence in depth: if the WAF misses an attack, the application still validates input.
Correct. Two-person control (separation of duties) stops one person exporting keys alone.
Opening everything, even briefly, abandons secure defaults and creates an exposure window.
Detailed errors leak internal information to attackers; production should fail quietly and log details internally.
Shared accounts destroy accountability and break individual access control.
questions.concept: Least privilege, defence in depth and separation of duties in practice.
questions.trap: Accepting convenience changes that quietly undo a principle.
questions.managerLens: Make design principles review criteria, so convenience shortcuts are visible and justified.
questions.practicalNote: Many teams keep a secure design checklist in their architecture review template.
questions.gap: Recognising design principles in concrete changes.

questions.stem: A company says it is moving to a zero trust architecture. Staff currently get broad access to internal applications once they connect to the corporate VPN. Which change BEST reflects zero trust?
options: Buy a larger VPN concentrator so that more staff can connect at once
Trust devices on the office LAN fully and require MFA only for remote access
Authorise each request to each app by user, device health and context
Require users to sign in with MFA once a day at the start of their work
rationales: A bigger VPN keeps the same network-based trust model.
Trusting the office LAN is exactly the location-based trust zero trust removes.
Correct. Zero trust removes implicit trust from network location: each access decision checks identity, device posture and context, per application.
Daily MFA is good hygiene, but a single check that then grants broad access is still perimeter thinking.
questions.concept: Zero trust: per-request, per-resource decisions based on identity, device and context.
questions.trap: Equating zero trust with MFA or a better VPN.
questions.managerLens: Zero trust is a journey; start with the most valuable applications and strongest identity controls.
questions.practicalNote: NIST SP 800-207 describes zero trust with policy decision and enforcement points in front of each resource.

questions.stem: A medical device maker wants a rule that stops data from low-integrity sources, such as unverified field reports, from altering its high-integrity calibration database. Which model's rules address this directly?
options: Biba integrity model
Bell-LaPadula model
Brewer-Nash model
Graham-Denning model
rationales: Correct. Biba protects integrity: subjects may not write up to higher integrity levels, so low-integrity sources cannot corrupt high-integrity data.
Bell-LaPadula is about confidentiality and actually allows writing up.
Brewer-Nash prevents conflicts of interest between competing clients.
Graham-Denning defines rules for creating and deleting subjects and objects and managing rights, not integrity levels.
questions.concept: Biba: no write up, no read down, to protect integrity.
questions.trap: Choosing Bell-LaPadula because it is the best-known model.
questions.managerLens: Start from the protection goal: integrity points to Biba or Clark-Wilson.
questions.practicalNote: Windows Mandatory Integrity Control uses integrity levels in a Biba-like way to limit what low-integrity processes can change.
questions.gap: Linking models to their security goals.

questions.stem: At an audit firm, an analyst who has opened files for one mobile network operator is automatically blocked from opening files for that operator's direct competitor, though she may still open files for a bank. Which model does this implement?
options: Clark-Wilson model
Biba model
Take-Grant model
Brewer-Nash model
rationales: Clark-Wilson enforces integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties, not conflict-of-interest rules.
Biba controls integrity levels, not access based on what a user has already seen.
Take-Grant models how rights are passed between subjects.
Correct. Brewer-Nash (the Chinese Wall) changes access dynamically based on history to prevent conflicts of interest.
questions.concept: Brewer-Nash: access depends on what you have already accessed.
questions.trap: Thinking every access model is static.
questions.managerLens: Consultancies and auditors use Chinese Walls to manage client confidentiality and conflicts.
questions.practicalNote: Ethical walls in legal and audit document systems implement this automatically.

questions.stem: A retailer's public price list website holds no confidential data, but a wrong price displayed for even an hour costs it money and causes complaints. The site must also stay available during sales. Where should control effort focus FIRST?
options: Encrypting the price database at rest with keys in a separate HSM
Change control and integrity monitoring for the published prices
Data loss prevention on the web servers to stop prices leaking out
Classifying the price list as Confidential and limiting who can view it
rationales: Encryption at rest protects confidentiality, which matters little for public data.
Correct. The requirement is integrity (and availability): controlled, approved changes and detection of unauthorised changes address the real impact.
The prices are public; preventing leakage is pointless.
Restricting views contradicts the purpose of a public price list.
questions.concept: Select controls from the requirement: here integrity, not confidentiality.
questions.trap: Defaulting to encryption whatever the requirement.
questions.managerLens: Spend where the impact is; categorise C, I and A separately.
questions.practicalNote: File integrity monitoring and approval workflows in the content system are typical controls for this case.
questions.gap: Deriving controls from C, I and A requirements.

questions.stem: A government department is choosing between two firewalls that both hold Common Criteria certificates, one at EAL2 and one at EAL4. Which TWO statements about Common Criteria are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The EAL shows how thoroughly the product was evaluated, not how strong its security is
Products are evaluated against a security target, often based on a protection profile
An EAL7 product is the most secure product available in its category
A certificate stays valid for later versions of the product too
Common Criteria applies to hardware products only, not to software
rationales: Correct. A higher EAL means deeper evaluation and more assurance in the claims, not stronger features.
Correct. The vendor's security target states the claims; protection profiles standardise requirements for a product type.
EAL7 means formally verified evaluation of the claims, not that the product is the most secure.
Certificates apply to the evaluated version and configuration only.
Common Criteria covers software, hardware and firmware products.
questions.concept: Common Criteria measures assurance in stated claims; EAL is evaluation depth.
questions.trap: Reading EAL as a security strength score.
questions.managerLens: Check the security target matches your needs and the evaluated configuration matches your deployment.
questions.practicalNote: The Common Criteria portal lists certified products, their security targets and evaluated configurations.

questions.stem: A bank is setting up an internal certificate authority. Its root signing key must be generated and used only inside a tamper-resistant device, with dual control over its use. Which component is designed for this?
options: The TPM chip on the CA server's motherboard
A secure enclave in an administrator's smartphone
A hardware security module with dual-control access
An encrypted software keystore on the CA server
rationales: A TPM protects keys tied to one platform, mainly for boot integrity and sealed storage; it is not built for CA operations with dual control.
A phone enclave protects the phone's own keys, not an enterprise root CA.
Correct. HSMs are tamper-resistant devices built to generate, store and use high-value keys, with role separation, quorum controls and audit.
Software keystores can be copied if the server is compromised; they do not provide tamper resistance.
questions.concept: HSMs protect high-value keys; TPMs protect a platform's integrity and its own keys.
questions.trap: Choosing the TPM because it is also 'trusted hardware'.
questions.managerLens: Match the protection to the key's value: root CA keys justify HSMs and key ceremonies.
questions.practicalNote: Root CA keys are often kept offline in an HSM and used only in recorded key ceremonies.

questions.stem: An attacker exploits a buffer overflow in a legacy service to place shellcode on the stack and jump to it. Which operating system feature is designed to stop that injected code from running?
options: Data execution prevention marking the stack non-executable
Address space layout randomisation of the service's memory
Measured boot using the platform's TPM
Running the service in its own user account
rationales: Correct. DEP/NX marks data areas such as the stack as non-executable, so the processor refuses to run code placed there.
ASLR makes it harder to find the right address, but it does not stop code from executing where it lands.
Measured boot verifies the boot chain; it does not affect a running service's memory.
A separate account limits the damage after exploitation, not the execution of the injected code.
questions.concept: DEP/NX prevents execution in data areas; ASLR makes targeting harder. They work together.
questions.trap: Choosing ASLR because it is the better-known mitigation.
questions.managerLens: Require modern exploit mitigations on legacy services, or isolate the services that cannot use them.
questions.practicalNote: Attackers bypass DEP with return-oriented programming, which is why DEP and ASLR are used together.
questions.gap: Knowing what each memory protection feature does.

questions.stem: A company is standardising on laptops with TPM 2.0 chips. Which TWO are typical uses of the TPM? (Select TWO.)
options: Protecting the disk encryption key so it is released only if the boot state is unchanged
Recording boot measurements so the laptop's integrity can be attested to a server
Offloading TLS encryption for the company's high-traffic web servers
Storing the passwords users save for websites in their browsers
Scanning files on the laptop for known malware signatures
rationales: Correct. Sealing the disk encryption key to the TPM means a tampered boot chain cannot unlock the disk.
Correct. Measured boot records hashes in the TPM so a server can check the device before granting access.
Bulk TLS offload is a job for accelerators or HSMs, not a laptop's TPM.
Browser password storage is handled by the browser or operating system, not by the TPM itself.
Malware scanning is software; the TPM does not inspect files.
questions.concept: TPMs seal keys to platform state and support attestation.
questions.trap: Assuming any security task can be given to the TPM.
questions.managerLens: Use TPM-backed disk encryption and device attestation as building blocks for zero trust.
questions.practicalNote: BitLocker uses the TPM to seal its key; device health attestation feeds conditional access decisions.
questions.gap: Knowing what a TPM is for.

questions.stem: A SaaS provider plans to run containers for many customers on shared hosts instead of giving each customer its own virtual machine. What is the MAIN additional security risk of this design?
options: Container images are larger than VM images and take longer to copy
Containers start more slowly than virtual machines during scaling
Each container needs its own public IP address on the internet
Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel flaw breaks isolation
rationales: Container images are usually smaller than VM images, and size is not a security risk.
Containers usually start faster; startup time is not a security concern here.
Containers do not each need a public IP address.
Correct. All containers on a host share one kernel; a kernel vulnerability or misconfiguration can let one tenant escape to the host or other tenants.
questions.concept: Containers isolate less strongly than VMs because they share the host kernel.
questions.trap: Focusing on operational differences instead of isolation.
questions.managerLens: For multi-tenant designs, decide the isolation strength the risk needs: hardened containers, sandboxed runtimes or VMs.
questions.practicalNote: Sandboxed runtimes and micro-VMs add a stronger boundary for untrusted multi-tenant workloads.

questions.subtopic: IoT devices that cannot be patched
questions.stem: A hotel installs 300 smart thermostats. They have hard-coded administrator credentials, and the vendor has said it will not release firmware updates. What is the BEST way to reduce the risk?
options: Install antivirus software on each thermostat before it goes live
Place the thermostats on an isolated network with tightly limited flows
Change the hard-coded credentials on each device through its web interface
Rely on the hotel's perimeter firewall to block attacks from outside
rationales: IoT devices like these cannot run antivirus software.
Correct. When devices cannot be fixed, isolate them: a separate network that can reach only the management service it needs.
Hard-coded credentials, by definition, cannot be changed.
The perimeter does not stop threats already inside, such as guests on the hotel network.
questions.concept: Unfixable devices are contained by segmentation.
questions.trap: Choosing an option that is impossible for the device.
questions.managerLens: Make security requirements part of IoT procurement; isolate what you cannot fix.
questions.practicalNote: Guest, corporate, payment and IoT networks are usually kept on separate VLANs or SSIDs with firewall rules between them.
questions.gap: Managing IoT that cannot be patched.

questions.stem: A fintech moves part of its application to serverless functions on a public cloud. Which security responsibility remains with the fintech?
options: Patching the operating system that the functions run on
Maintaining the physical servers in the provider's regions
The function code and the permissions granted to each function
Securing the hypervisor that isolates one tenant from another
rationales: In serverless, the provider manages and patches the runtime environment and OS.
Physical infrastructure always belongs to the provider.
Correct. The customer still owns its code, dependencies, data, and the identity permissions each function has.
Tenant isolation below the function is the provider's responsibility.
questions.concept: Serverless shrinks the customer's share to code, data and permissions, but not to zero.
questions.trap: Assuming serverless means the provider handles all security.
questions.managerLens: Focus serverless security on least-privilege function roles, secure code and dependency management.
questions.practicalNote: Over-permissive function roles are among the most common serverless weaknesses.
questions.gap: Knowing the customer's share in serverless.

questions.stem: HR analysts may only query average salaries by department. In departments with two or three staff, they have worked out individuals' salaries by comparing averages before and after a new hire. Which TWO controls address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Refuse queries whose result would cover fewer than a set number of people
Add small random noise to aggregate results so they cannot be differenced
Encrypt the salary database at rest with keys held in an HSM
Log every query the analysts run against the salary database
Require analysts to use stronger passwords for the HR system
rationales: Correct. A minimum query set size stops statistics that describe only a handful of people.
Correct. Perturbation (adding noise) prevents exact differencing while keeping aggregates useful.
Encryption at rest does not stop authorised queries from revealing information.
Logging may detect misuse later but does not prevent the inference.
Password strength does not affect what authorised analysts can deduce.
questions.concept: Inference attacks are countered by limiting or perturbing query results.
questions.trap: Applying access or encryption controls to a problem caused by authorised queries.
questions.managerLens: Treat statistical outputs about people as personal data when groups are small.
questions.practicalNote: Differential privacy formalises noise-adding so aggregate data can be released safely.

questions.stem: Why do protocols such as TLS use asymmetric cryptography to agree a key, and then a symmetric cipher for the data?
options: Symmetric ciphers cannot provide integrity for data in transit
Asymmetric solves key exchange; symmetric ciphers are much faster
Asymmetric algorithms need much shorter keys than symmetric ones
Symmetric keys cannot be changed during a session once agreed
rationales: Authenticated symmetric modes such as AES-GCM provide integrity as well as confidentiality.
Correct. Public-key methods let two parties agree a key without a shared secret, but they are slow; symmetric ciphers then encrypt the bulk data efficiently.
It is the reverse: asymmetric keys are much longer for comparable strength.
Session keys can be renegotiated; this is not why hybrids are used.
questions.concept: Hybrid cryptography: asymmetric for key exchange and signatures, symmetric for bulk data.
questions.trap: Mixing up which family is faster or needs longer keys.
questions.managerLens: Know the trade-offs well enough to judge vendor claims.
questions.practicalNote: TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral (EC)DHE for key exchange and AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for data.

questions.stem: An audit finds that the encryption key for a customer database is stored in a configuration file on the same server as the database. Developers propose fixes. Which BEST addresses the weakness?
options: Rotate the key monthly and keep the new key in the same configuration file
Switch to a longer key length, such as AES-256 instead of AES-128
Obfuscate the configuration file so that the key is harder to spot
Move the key to a key management service with separate access control
rationales: Rotation helps, but anyone who compromises the server still gets the current key.
Key length is not the problem; the key is sitting beside the data it protects.
Obfuscation is not protection; anyone with server access can recover the key.
Correct. Separating keys from data, with their own access control, logging and rotation, means a server compromise does not hand over both.
questions.concept: Keep keys separate from the data they protect.
questions.trap: Strengthening the algorithm when key storage is the weakness.
questions.managerLens: Make key management a platform service, not a decision for each application team.
questions.practicalNote: Cloud KMS services and HSMs provide envelope encryption, so applications never handle master keys.

questions.stem: A company learns that the private key for its customer portal's TLS certificate was copied by an attacker. The certificate is valid for another nine months. What should it do FIRST?
options: Revoke the certificate and replace it with a new key pair
Keep the certificate until it expires, then renew it as usual
Move the portal to a new IP address and update DNS records
Enable HTTP Strict Transport Security on the portal
rationales: Correct. With the key compromised, the attacker could impersonate the portal. Revoking the certificate and issuing a new one on a new key ends that.
Waiting nine months leaves an impersonation risk open the whole time.
A new address does not stop the attacker presenting the valid certificate from anywhere.
HSTS forces HTTPS but does not stop an attacker using the stolen key and certificate.
questions.concept: Key compromise requires revocation and re-keying.
questions.trap: Treating the certificate's expiry date as protection.
questions.managerLens: Have a tested procedure for emergency certificate replacement.
questions.practicalNote: Browsers check revocation inconsistently, so short certificate lifetimes are increasingly used as well.
questions.gap: Responding to key compromise in PKI.

questions.stem: A supplier sends a digitally signed contract PDF. The signature verifies against the supplier's certificate, which chains to a trusted CA. Which TWO things does this show? (Select TWO.)
options: The document has not been altered since it was signed
It was signed with the private key matching the supplier's certificate
The contents of the document were kept confidential in transit
The supplier's signatory read the document before signing it
The document was created on the date shown in its metadata
rationales: Correct. A valid signature means the signed content matches what was signed: integrity.
Correct. Only the holder of the private key could have produced it: authenticity and support for non-repudiation.
Signatures do not encrypt; confidentiality needs encryption.
Cryptography cannot show what a person read or intended.
Without a trusted timestamp, the signature does not prove when the document was created.
questions.concept: Digital signatures give integrity and origin, not confidentiality or proof of time.
questions.trap: Over-reading what a signature proves.
questions.managerLens: Add trusted timestamping when the time of signing matters legally.
questions.practicalNote: PAdES signatures with a timestamp authority are common for long-term signed PDFs.
questions.gap: Knowing what signatures do and do not prove.

questions.stem: An attacker has captured a company's encrypted emails and notices that every email ends with the same standard signature block, whose wording is published on the company's website. Which type of attack does this enable?
options: Chosen plaintext
Ciphertext only
Known plaintext
Chosen ciphertext
rationales: In a chosen plaintext attack the attacker picks plaintexts and gets them encrypted; here they simply know some plaintext.
The attacker has more than ciphertext: they know part of the plaintext.
Correct. Knowing both a piece of plaintext and its ciphertext is a known plaintext attack.
Chosen ciphertext attacks involve getting chosen ciphertexts decrypted.
questions.concept: Classify cryptanalytic attacks by what the attacker has.
questions.trap: Confusing known and chosen plaintext.
questions.managerLens: Modern ciphers resist known plaintext attacks; the risk is mostly in weak or home-made algorithms.
questions.practicalNote: Predictable message content helped break Enigma; modern algorithms are designed to withstand this.

questions.stem: Researchers recover a smart card's signing key by measuring tiny changes in its power use while it signs thousands of messages. Which category of attack is this?
options: Side-channel attack
Brute-force attack
Frequency analysis
Birthday attack
rationales: Correct. Power analysis extracts secrets from physical effects of the computation: a side-channel attack.
Brute force tries keys exhaustively; here the key leaks from the device.
Frequency analysis breaks simple substitution ciphers using letter frequencies.
A birthday attack finds hash collisions; it does not extract keys from hardware.
questions.concept: Side-channel attacks target the implementation, not the algorithm.
questions.trap: Assuming strong algorithms make the device secure.
questions.managerLens: Demand side-channel resistance evidence, such as Common Criteria evaluation, for cards and HSMs.
questions.practicalNote: Constant-time code, masking and noise generation are standard side-channel countermeasures.

questions.stem: After compromising a workstation, an attacker extracts NTLM password hashes from memory and uses them directly to authenticate to file servers, without cracking any of them. What is this technique?
options: Golden ticket
Pass the hash
Rainbow table attack
Credential stuffing
rationales: A golden ticket is a forged Kerberos ticket made with the KRBTGT account's key.
Correct. Pass the hash uses the hash itself as the credential, so cracking is unnecessary.
Rainbow tables crack hashes back to passwords; this attacker never cracks them.
Credential stuffing reuses username and password pairs leaked from other sites.
questions.concept: Pass the hash: the hash is enough to authenticate with NTLM.
questions.trap: Assuming a hash must be cracked before it is useful.
questions.managerLens: Reduce exposure with privileged access workstations, LAPS, Credential Guard and less NTLM use.
questions.practicalNote: Tiered administration keeps domain admin credentials off ordinary workstations where they could be harvested.

questions.stem: A bank applies crime prevention through environmental design to its new branch. Which design feature is an example of natural surveillance?
options: A fence with a single controlled gate around the car park
Bollards along the front to stop vehicles reaching the entrance
Signs and paving that mark where public space ends
Windows and lighting that let people see the car park
rationales: A fence with one gate is natural access control.
Bollards are a physical barrier against vehicles.
Marking boundaries is territorial reinforcement.
Correct. Natural surveillance is design that lets people see activity, which discourages crime.
questions.concept: CPTED: natural surveillance, natural access control, territorial reinforcement.
questions.trap: Mixing up the three CPTED strategies.
questions.managerLens: Build security into site design early; it is cheaper than adding guards later.
questions.practicalNote: Low landscaping and good lighting along walkways are classic natural surveillance measures.

questions.stem: A bank is choosing a site for a new data centre. Which TWO factors matter MOST from a security and resilience point of view? (Select TWO.)
options: Exposure to floods and other natural hazards
Access to diverse power and telecom routes
Short travel time for executives at head office
Low rent compared with other available sites
Prominent signs that show it is the bank's data centre
rationales: Correct. Natural hazards such as flooding can take the whole site down.
Correct. Independent utility and telecom paths avoid single points of failure.
Executive convenience is not a security or resilience factor.
Cost matters to the business, but it is not a security factor.
Advertising the site makes it a target; data centres are usually kept low-profile.
questions.concept: Site selection weighs hazards, utilities, access and visibility.
questions.trap: Letting convenience or cost stand in for security factors.
questions.managerLens: Put hazard and dependency analysis in front of property decisions.
questions.practicalNote: Flood maps, seismic data and utility route surveys are standard inputs to data centre site selection.
questions.gap: Knowing what matters in site selection.

questions.stem: Magnetic locks secure the exit doors of a staffed data hall. The design team must decide how the locks behave when the fire alarm sounds. What should happen?
options: Stay locked until a guard confirms that there really is a fire
Stay locked, because the servers inside must be protected
Unlock for exit, because people's safety comes before the assets
Unlock only for staff whose badges are cleared for the data hall
rationales: Delaying exit until someone confirms the fire puts lives at risk.
Equipment can be replaced; people cannot. Protecting assets never outranks life safety.
Correct. Exit doors must fail safe (unlock) in an emergency; assets are protected by other means such as cameras and door alarms.
Badge checks in a fire delay escape and may trap visitors or contractors.
questions.concept: Life safety first: emergency exits fail safe.
questions.trap: Choosing fail-secure for an exit because the room holds valuable equipment.
questions.managerLens: No security control may compromise safe escape; fire codes usually require it too.
questions.practicalNote: Exit doors often combine fail-safe locks, a local alarm on opening and camera coverage.

questions.stem: During Harare's dry season, monitoring shows relative humidity in a server room falling to 15%. What is the MAIN risk to the equipment?
options: Condensation forming on circuit boards
Corrosion of metal connectors and contacts
Electrostatic discharge damaging components
Overheating of the processors in the servers
rationales: Condensation is a risk of high humidity, not low.
Corrosion is also a high-humidity problem.
Correct. Very dry air lets static build up, and discharge can damage electronic components.
Humidity does not directly cause processors to overheat; temperature and airflow do.
questions.concept: Low humidity causes static; high humidity causes condensation and corrosion.
questions.trap: Mixing up the effects of low and high humidity.
questions.managerLens: Monitor temperature and humidity with alerts, not just air conditioning.
questions.practicalNote: ASHRAE guidance gives recommended temperature and humidity ranges for data centres.

questions.stem: An internal HR system was approved for use two years ago, when it was reachable only from the office network. The business now wants staff to use it from home over the internet. What should happen BEFORE the change goes live?
options: Nothing, since the system was already approved and is running well
Run a full penetration test first, then make the change at once
Move it behind the VPN, since that keeps it off the open internet
Analyse the change's security impact and have the owner re-accept risk
rationales: The original approval assumed internal-only access; a major change in exposure invalidates that assumption.
Testing is useful evidence, but it does not replace analysis of new requirements and an owner's decision.
A VPN may be one answer, but choosing it skips the analysis of what the change needs.
Correct. A significant change triggers a security impact analysis, updated controls and fresh acceptance of the residual risk.
questions.concept: Significant changes in operation trigger impact analysis and re-authorisation.
questions.trap: Treating an earlier approval as permanent.
questions.managerLens: Tie change management to security review for changes that alter exposure.
questions.practicalNote: In NIST's RMF, significant changes trigger reassessment and possibly re-authorisation.
questions.gap: Managing security through the operational lifecycle.

questions.stem: A company is decommissioning an old customer portal after moving its users to a new platform. Which TWO steps belong in the decommissioning plan? (Select TWO.)
options: Archive data the retention schedule requires, then sanitise the remaining storage
Revoke the portal's service accounts, certificates and firewall rules
Keep the portal's virtual machine powered off indefinitely just in case
Delete the portal's security logs on the day it is switched off
Reuse the portal's public IP address for a new service without review
rationales: Correct. Retained data is archived as required; everything else is sanitised.
Correct. Leftover accounts, certificates and firewall rules are common footholds for attackers.
A dormant VM still holds data and credentials, and may be restarted unpatched.
Logs may be needed for investigations and are usually under retention rules.
Old DNS records or partner allow-lists may still point at the address.
questions.concept: Retirement removes data, access and trust relationships, not just the server.
questions.trap: Switching a system off and calling it retired.
questions.managerLens: Use a decommissioning checklist with sign-off by the system owner.
questions.practicalNote: Dangling DNS records pointing at released cloud addresses enable subdomain takeover.
questions.gap: Knowing the steps of secure retirement.

questions.stem: An attacker exploited a public web server in a retailer's data centre, then moved laterally to the database and payment servers on the same flat server network. The perimeter next-generation firewall is due for renewal next quarter, and the vendor is offering a larger model at a discount. Which change would MOST reduce the impact of a similar compromise?
options: Upgrade to the larger perimeter firewall and enable its intrusion prevention.
Put each department's servers in a separate VLAN with routing between them.
Micro-segment workloads so only required flows between servers are allowed.
Add a network IDS on the internet link to alert on exploitation attempts.
rationales: The perimeter firewall inspects north-south traffic. The damage came from east-west movement inside the data centre, which it does not see. The discount is a decoy.
Coarse segmentation helps a little, but servers that talk to each other often share a VLAN, and routing between VLANs is usually permissive unless it is filtered.
Correct. Default-deny rules between workloads limit an attacker on one server to the flows that server genuinely needs, which contains lateral movement.
Detection at the edge may spot the initial exploit, but it neither prevents nor limits movement inside the network.
questions.concept: East-west traffic control: micro-segmentation limits lateral movement.
questions.trap: Investing in the perimeter when the problem is inside it.
questions.managerLens: Spend where the attack path actually ran; tie the investment to the incident's root cause, not to a vendor offer.
questions.practicalNote: Micro-segmentation is usually built with host firewalls, hypervisor distributed firewalls or SDN policy, starting with high-value assets such as payment systems.
questions.gap: Not distinguishing north-south from east-west traffic and the controls for each.

questions.stem: Network engineers now work partly from home and need to manage the company's core routers and switches. Which design BEST protects the management plane?
options: Reach a dedicated management network through a hardened jump host with MFA.
Expose SSH on the routers' internet interfaces and require key-based logins.
Use Telnet inside the corporate remote-access VPN, which encrypts the traffic.
Let the vendor's cloud portal push changes once they are approved by e-mail.
rationales: Correct. A separate management network, reached only through a monitored jump host with strong authentication, keeps device administration off user networks and the internet.
Keys are better than passwords, but exposing management services to the internet invites scanning, brute force and exploitation of SSH or device vulnerabilities.
The VPN protects only the path to the corporate edge. Telnet then sends credentials in clear text across internal segments, and management stays reachable from user networks.
E-mail approval is weak authorisation, and the design gives a third party write access to core devices without strong controls.
questions.concept: Protect the management plane with isolation and strong, monitored access.
questions.trap: Believing that encrypting one hop, or key authentication alone, makes exposed management acceptable.
questions.managerLens: Administrative access to core infrastructure is high impact; require isolation, MFA and logging by policy.
questions.practicalNote: Common designs use an out-of-band management network or VRF, a bastion or privileged access workstation, and TACACS+ or RADIUS with MFA.
questions.gap: Not separating the management plane from user and data traffic.

questions.stem: Mosi's board approves replacing the branch MPLS circuits with SD-WAN over ordinary internet links. Which design requirement matters MOST for security?
options: Buy the highest-bandwidth internet links available at each branch site
Encrypt and authenticate the tunnels; lock down the controller
Keep one MPLS circuit at head office as a backup path for branch traffic
Give each branch its own internet breakout so that cloud apps are faster
rationales: Bandwidth affects performance, not the security of traffic crossing the internet.
Correct. The internet path is untrusted, so tunnels must be encrypted and authenticated (usually IPsec), and the controller, which pushes policy to every site, must be tightly protected.
A backup path helps availability but does nothing for the confidentiality of traffic on the new links.
Local breakout can improve performance but spreads inspection points; it is not the main security requirement.
questions.concept: SD-WAN moves traffic onto untrusted networks; encryption and controller security become essential.
questions.trap: Treating the change as a performance project.
questions.managerLens: Cost savings that change the trust model need security requirements written into the design.
questions.practicalNote: SD-WAN controllers and orchestrators are high-value targets; protect them like domain controllers.
questions.gap: Recognising how moving off a private WAN changes risk.

questions.stem: Mosi's IP desk phones share the flat office network with PCs, and calls travel unencrypted. Which TWO changes BEST protect voice traffic? (Select TWO.)
options: Put the phones on a separate voice VLAN with limited flows to the call server
Encrypt call signalling with TLS and the media streams with SRTP
Give the phones public IP addresses so remote staff can reach them
Turn off quality of service so that voice and data are treated alike
Allow the phones to reach the internet directly for firmware updates
rationales: Correct. A voice VLAN separates phones from PCs, limiting eavesdropping and attacks from compromised computers.
Correct. TLS protects call set-up and SRTP protects the audio itself from interception.
Public addresses expose phones to the internet, inviting attacks and toll fraud.
Removing QoS harms call quality and adds nothing to security.
Direct internet access widens exposure; updates should come from a managed internal source.
questions.concept: VoIP security: separate voice traffic and encrypt signalling and media.
questions.trap: Choosing changes that improve reach or simplicity at the expense of exposure.
questions.managerLens: Voice is data: give it the same segmentation and encryption thinking.
questions.practicalNote: Many IP phones support a voice VLAN assigned automatically by the switch, plus SRTP when the call server enables it.

questions.stem: Any device plugged into a Mosi wall port, including a visitor's laptop, gets an internal address and can reach internal servers. Which control BEST fixes this?
options: Disable unused wall ports and enable them on request
Keep a list of approved MAC addresses on each access switch
Use 802.1X so only authenticated, compliant devices join
Ask visitors to sign a register before they plug in their laptops
rationales: Disabling unused ports helps, but any active port, such as a desk or meeting-room port, still admits any device.
MAC addresses are trivially spoofed and allow-lists are hard to maintain at scale.
Correct. 802.1X-based NAC authenticates the device or user before granting access, and can place unknown devices in a guest VLAN and check device posture.
A register records visitors but does not stop their devices reaching servers.
questions.concept: NAC with 802.1X controls who and what connects to the network.
questions.trap: Choosing a partial or easily bypassed control.
questions.managerLens: Treat physical ports as network entry points and control them centrally.
questions.practicalNote: Devices that cannot do 802.1X, such as printers, are usually handled with MAC authentication bypass plus profiling and restricted VLANs.
questions.gap: Knowing how NAC works and why it beats MAC filtering.

questions.stem: An attacker on an office LAN sends forged ARP replies so that traffic meant for the default gateway is sent to the attacker's laptop instead. At which OSI layer does this attack operate?
options: Layer 2, data link
Layer 3, network
Layer 4, transport
Layer 7, application
rationales: Correct. ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local segment, a data link layer function, and poisoning it redirects frames.
IP routing is layer 3, but ARP spoofing manipulates the layer 2 address mapping.
Layer 4 deals with ports and sessions such as TCP and UDP.
Application-layer attacks target services such as HTTP or DNS content.
questions.concept: ARP spoofing is a layer 2 attack.
questions.trap: Choosing layer 3 because IP addresses are involved.
questions.managerLens: Map threats to layers so controls are placed where they work.
questions.practicalNote: Dynamic ARP inspection and DHCP snooping on managed switches stop ARP spoofing.
questions.gap: Placing attacks on the OSI model.

questions.stem: A web server stops accepting new connections. Monitoring shows thousands of half-open TCP connections from spoofed addresses that never complete. Which mechanism is the attack abusing?
options: The DNS lookup the client makes before it connects
The TLS handshake that negotiates the session keys
The HTTP keep-alive setting on the web server
The TCP three-way handshake used to open connections
rationales: DNS resolution happens before connecting and is not involved in half-open TCP connections.
TLS begins only after the TCP connection is established, which never happens here.
Keep-alive affects established connections, not half-open ones.
Correct. A SYN flood sends SYNs and never completes the handshake, filling the server's table of half-open connections.
questions.concept: SYN floods exhaust the server's half-open connection queue.
questions.trap: Choosing a higher-layer protocol that never starts.
questions.managerLens: Plan DDoS resilience with the provider; on-premises fixes have limits.
questions.practicalNote: SYN cookies, upstream scrubbing and CDN fronting are standard defences.

questions.stem: Two offices connect their networks through firewalls over the internet. The traffic between them must be confidential, and internal IP addresses should not be visible to anyone watching the internet link. Which IPsec configuration fits?
options: AH in transport mode between the two firewalls
ESP in tunnel mode between the two firewalls
ESP in transport mode between each pair of hosts
AH in tunnel mode between the two firewalls
rationales: AH gives integrity and authentication but no confidentiality, and transport mode leaves the original IP header exposed.
Correct. ESP encrypts, and tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet, hiding internal addresses. It is the standard site-to-site choice.
Host-to-host transport mode does not suit gateway-to-gateway links and exposes the original addresses.
AH provides no encryption, so the traffic would not be confidential.
questions.concept: Site-to-site VPNs use ESP in tunnel mode.
questions.trap: Choosing AH, which never encrypts.
questions.managerLens: Standardise VPN configurations so gateways are not left on weak settings.
questions.practicalNote: IKEv2 with AES-GCM is a common modern configuration for site-to-site IPsec.

questions.stem: A bank is deciding whether to disable TLS 1.2 on its customer portal and allow TLS 1.3 only. Which TWO are genuine security benefits of TLS 1.3? (Select TWO.)
options: Every handshake uses ephemeral key exchange, giving forward secrecy
Legacy options such as static RSA key exchange and CBC ciphers are removed
Each client must present its own certificate to the server
DNS lookups for the portal are encrypted automatically
Message integrity is provided by the AH protocol
rationales: Correct. TLS 1.3 removed static key exchange, so a stolen server key cannot decrypt recorded past sessions.
Correct. Weak and legacy algorithms were removed, shrinking the attack surface for downgrade and padding attacks.
Client certificates remain optional in TLS 1.3.
TLS protects the connection to the portal; DNS privacy needs DNS over HTTPS or TLS.
AH is part of IPsec, not TLS; TLS 1.3 uses AEAD ciphers for integrity.
questions.concept: TLS 1.3 mandates forward secrecy and removes legacy cryptography.
questions.trap: Crediting TLS with protections it does not provide.
questions.managerLens: Weigh the benefit against older clients that may be cut off.
questions.practicalNote: Most banks keep TLS 1.2 with strong cipher suites alongside TLS 1.3 while older clients remain.

questions.stem: A hospital's virtual servers use iSCSI to reach a storage array. The iSCSI traffic currently shares the same VLAN as user PCs. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Move iSCSI to a dedicated storage network and require CHAP authentication
Raise the MTU on the user VLAN so storage traffic runs more efficiently
Put the storage array's management page behind the internet firewall
Replace iSCSI with SMB file shares, which are more widely understood
rationales: Correct. iSCSI carries raw disk blocks; isolating it on its own network and authenticating initiators keeps users from reading or tampering with storage traffic.
MTU tuning is performance work and leaves storage exposed to users.
The management interface matters, but the exposure here is the storage traffic itself on the user network.
Changing protocol does not remove the need to separate and protect storage traffic.
questions.concept: Converged protocols such as iSCSI need isolation and authentication.
questions.trap: Treating storage traffic as just another flow on the user network.
questions.managerLens: Classify storage networks as high-value infrastructure.
questions.practicalNote: Storage networks are typically separate VLANs or physical fabrics, sometimes with IPsec for iSCSI.

questions.stem: A penetration tester reached the finance VLAN from a user access port by negotiating a trunk with the switch. Which TWO switch changes BEST prevent VLAN hopping? (Select TWO.)
options: Disable automatic trunk negotiation and set user ports to access mode
Set the native VLAN on trunks to an unused VLAN that carries no traffic
Enable DHCP snooping on every user-facing access port
Increase the MTU on trunk links between the core switches
Turn on PortFast on the uplinks between the switches
rationales: Correct. Switch spoofing works by negotiating a trunk; forcing access mode and disabling negotiation stops it.
Correct. Double-tagging attacks rely on the native VLAN; moving it to an unused VLAN defeats them.
DHCP snooping stops rogue DHCP servers, not VLAN hopping.
MTU size affects frame size and performance; it has no effect on separation between VLANs.
PortFast speeds up edge ports and is unsafe on switch uplinks; it does not address hopping.
questions.concept: VLAN hopping is stopped by disabling trunk negotiation and isolating the native VLAN.
questions.trap: Picking a valid switch security feature that addresses a different attack.
questions.managerLens: Harden switch configurations with a baseline, not port by port.
questions.practicalNote: Configuration compliance tools can check every switch against the hardening baseline.

questions.stem: A law firm's staff Wi-Fi uses WPA2 with one shared passphrase that has not changed since 2019. Several former employees still know it. What is the BEST replacement for staff access?
options: WPA2 with a new shared passphrase changed every quarter
Hiding the network name so it does not appear in scans
WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and individual credentials
MAC address filtering on the firm's wireless access points
rationales: Rotating a shared secret still lets every user, and anyone they tell, in; leavers keep access until the next change.
