Hidden networks are still easy to discover and add no authentication.
Correct. Enterprise mode gives each person their own credentials, so access can be revoked individually and activity attributed.
MAC addresses are easily spoofed and offer no real authentication.
questions.concept: Enterprise Wi-Fi with 802.1X replaces shared secrets with individual credentials.
questions.trap: Improving a shared secret instead of replacing it.
questions.managerLens: Tie network access to identity so leavers lose it automatically.
questions.practicalNote: WPA3-Personal (SAE) is the better choice where enterprise authentication is not possible, such as small sites.

questions.stem: Staff at an airport lounge connect to an access point broadcasting the company's network name. It is an attacker's evil twin, and several laptops send their credentials to it. The company uses 802.1X with PEAP. What MOST likely made this possible?
options: The company's access points broadcast their network name openly
The laptops were not set to require patches before connecting
Users had weak passwords that the attacker could guess offline
The laptops did not validate the authentication server's certificate
rationales: Hiding the name would not help; an attacker can copy any network name.
Patch status does not stop a laptop authenticating to a fake access point.
Password strength affects cracking afterwards; it does not explain why laptops trusted the fake network.
Correct. If clients do not check that the RADIUS server's certificate is the company's, they will run PEAP with any server, handing credentials to the evil twin.
questions.concept: 802.1X clients must validate the server certificate to defeat evil twins.
questions.trap: Assuming enterprise Wi-Fi is safe however clients are configured.
questions.managerLens: Push wireless profiles centrally, with certificate validation enforced.
questions.practicalNote: EAP-TLS with device certificates avoids sending passwords at all.
questions.gap: Understanding how enterprise Wi-Fi is attacked.

questions.stem: An attacker in a café copies contacts and calendar entries from a nearby phone over Bluetooth, without the owner noticing. What is this attack called?
options: Bluejacking
Bluebugging
War driving
Bluesnarfing
rationales: Bluejacking sends unsolicited messages; it does not take data.
Bluebugging takes control of the device, for example to make calls, rather than simply copying data.
War driving searches for Wi-Fi networks.
Correct. Bluesnarfing is unauthorised access to data on a device over Bluetooth.
questions.concept: Bluesnarfing steals data; bluejacking sends messages; bluebugging takes control.
questions.trap: Mixing up the Bluetooth attack names.
questions.managerLens: Set mobile device policy to keep Bluetooth non-discoverable and patched.
questions.practicalNote: Modern phones resist the classic attacks, but unpatched devices and IoT gadgets remain exposed.

questions.stem: A security manager is briefing executives who travel to regions where fake mobile base stations ('IMSI catchers') are used to track people. Which statement about 5G compared with 4G is correct?
options: 5G encrypts the subscriber's permanent ID before it goes over the air
5G encrypts every call end to end so the operator cannot listen to it
5G phones refuse to connect to any 4G network while abroad
5G removes the need for a SIM card or any subscriber authentication
rationales: Correct. 5G conceals the permanent identifier (SUPI) as a SUCI using the home network's public key, which defeats simple IMSI catching on 5G.
Radio-link encryption ends at the operator; 5G does not make calls end-to-end encrypted.
Phones fall back to older networks, which is how downgrade attacks expose identifiers.
5G still uses SIM or eSIM credentials and mutual authentication.
questions.concept: 5G conceals subscriber identity over the air; downgrades to older networks remain a risk.
questions.trap: Assuming 5G gives end-to-end call encryption.
questions.managerLens: For high-risk travel, add end-to-end encrypted apps and consider disabling 2G fallback.
questions.practicalNote: Some phones let users turn off 2G, which blocks the easiest downgrade attacks.
questions.gap: Knowing what cellular security does and does not protect.

questions.stem: An online retailer puts its website behind a CDN with DDoS protection. A week later, attackers flood the origin server directly and take the site down. Which TWO measures would have made the CDN protection effective? (Select TWO.)
options: Allow traffic to the origin from the CDN's address ranges and block the rest
Move the origin to an address that is not published in DNS or elsewhere
Shorten the CDN cache lifetime so content is always fresh
Turn off the CDN's web application firewall to reduce latency
Add more DNS records pointing customers at the origin directly
rationales: Correct. If the origin accepts only CDN traffic, attackers cannot bypass the CDN.
Correct. Once the origin's address leaked, it had to change; keeping it unpublished stops direct targeting.
Shorter caching sends more requests to the origin and weakens protection.
Removing the WAF lowers protection and does nothing about direct attacks.
Publishing the origin invites exactly this bypass.
questions.concept: A CDN only protects an origin that cannot be reached around it.
questions.trap: Assuming a CDN protects whatever is behind it.
questions.managerLens: Validate protections by testing the bypass paths, not just the front door.
questions.practicalNote: Old DNS records, mail headers and certificate transparency logs often leak origin addresses.

questions.stem: A data centre moves to software-defined networking, with a central controller programming all switches through APIs. Which component becomes the MOST critical to protect?
options: The individual top-of-rack switches in each row
The patch cables between the servers and switches
The SDN controller and its northbound APIs
The out-of-hours console ports on each switch
rationales: Individual switches follow the controller; compromising one affects less than compromising the controller.
Cabling matters physically but is not where SDN concentrates risk.
Correct. The controller decides how traffic flows everywhere; whoever controls it controls the network.
Console ports need protection, but the controller is the single point of control.
questions.concept: SDN centralises the control plane; the controller is the crown jewel.
questions.trap: Thinking of network security device by device.
questions.managerLens: Protect central control points with the strongest access control and monitoring.
questions.practicalNote: Controller APIs need strong authentication, role-based access and change logging.

questions.stem: In its cloud VPC, a team allows inbound HTTPS to web servers through a security group, and is surprised that responses reach clients without an outbound rule. A network ACL on the subnet needed explicit rules both ways. Why the difference?
options: Network ACLs are applied to individual instances
Security groups are stateful; network ACLs are stateless
Security groups apply only to outbound traffic
Network ACLs inspect application-layer content
rationales: It is security groups that attach to instances; network ACLs apply to subnets.
Correct. A stateful security group allows return traffic for permitted connections automatically; a stateless ACL needs rules in both directions.
Security groups control inbound and outbound traffic.
Network ACLs filter on addresses, protocols and ports, not application content.
questions.concept: Stateful filters allow return traffic; stateless filters need rules both ways.
questions.trap: Mixing up which cloud filter is stateful.
questions.managerLens: Standardise cloud network rules in templates so teams do not learn by trial and error.
questions.practicalNote: Infrastructure-as-code reviews catch overly broad security group rules before deployment.

questions.stem: After a breach that moved between servers unnoticed, a company wants visibility of east-west traffic inside its data centre. Which TWO sources give that visibility? (Select TWO.)
options: Flow records (NetFlow or IPFIX) exported from the internal switches
A network tap or SPAN feed from the core into a detection sensor
An IDS placed on the internet link outside the perimeter firewall
A web application firewall in front of the public website
Syslog from the internet edge router's interface counters
rationales: Correct. Flow records from internal switches show who talks to whom inside the data centre.
Correct. Copying core traffic to a sensor allows deep inspection of internal flows.
An internet-facing IDS sees north-south traffic only.
A WAF sees traffic to the public website, not server-to-server movement.
Edge router counters describe internet traffic volume, not internal flows.
questions.concept: East-west visibility needs internal telemetry: flows and packet capture from inside.
questions.trap: Choosing perimeter tools for internal problems.
questions.managerLens: Place sensors where the attack path runs.
questions.practicalNote: Network detection and response tools combine flow data and packet capture to spot lateral movement.

questions.stem: A power utility keeps its grid control network physically air-gapped from all other networks. Investigators later find malware on it. What was the MOST likely way in?
options: A wireless signal picked up from the office network
A routing error that briefly connected it to the internet
A brute-force attack on its firewall from outside
Removable media or a laptop connected by an engineer
rationales: A true air gap has no wireless link to bridge.
There is no routing path to make an error on if the gap is real.
An air-gapped network has no external firewall to attack.
Correct. Air gaps are usually crossed by people: USB drives, maintenance laptops and update media.
questions.concept: Air gaps are bridged by removable media and visiting devices.
questions.trap: Thinking an air gap needs no further controls.
questions.managerLens: Control media and maintenance devices as strictly as network connections.
questions.practicalNote: Media scanning kiosks and dedicated, clean maintenance laptops are common controls.

questions.stem: Users complain that VoIP calls sound choppy, with words arriving garbled, even though there is plenty of spare bandwidth. Which metric is MOST likely the problem?
options: Jitter
Throughput
Bandwidth
Packet size
rationales: Correct. Jitter is variation in packet delay; voice needs packets to arrive at a steady pace.
Throughput is fine; the link has spare capacity.
The link has spare bandwidth, so lack of capacity cannot explain the choppy audio.
Voice packets are small and fixed in size; size is not the issue.
questions.concept: Jitter is variation in delay; real-time media is sensitive to it.
questions.trap: Blaming bandwidth for every quality problem.
questions.managerLens: Availability includes quality: real-time services need QoS.
questions.practicalNote: QoS marking and jitter buffers in phones address jitter.

questions.stem: A defence contractor is cabling a new secure facility next to an electrical substation. Which cabling BEST resists both electromagnetic interference and tapping?
options: Unshielded copper (UTP)
Shielded copper (STP)
Fibre optic cable
Coaxial copper cable
rationales: UTP is the most vulnerable to interference and emanations.
Shielding helps with interference, but copper still radiates and can be tapped.
Correct. Light in glass is immune to electromagnetic interference and very hard to tap without detection.
Coax resists some interference but is copper and can be tapped.
questions.concept: Fibre resists EMI and tapping; copper does not.
questions.trap: Choosing shielded copper as good enough.
questions.managerLens: Match media to the threat and the environment.
questions.practicalNote: Fibre also supports longer runs, useful between buildings.

questions.stem: A university is deploying network access control for its staff network. Which TWO checks can NAC enforce before a device joins? (Select TWO.)
options: That the user or device has authenticated through 802.1X
That the device meets posture rules such as current patches
That web applications validate their input fields properly
That outgoing email passes SPF and DKIM checks
That documents on the device carry classification labels
rationales: Correct. NAC authenticates users or devices before granting network access.
Correct. Posture checks verify patch level, antivirus or encryption status.
Input validation is an application concern, not a network admission check.
Email authentication is handled by mail systems, not NAC.
Document labelling is a data protection matter, not a condition for network access.
questions.concept: NAC checks identity and device health at connection time.
questions.trap: Expecting NAC to enforce unrelated controls.
questions.managerLens: Use NAC to keep unknown and unhealthy devices off sensitive networks.
questions.practicalNote: Non-compliant devices are usually sent to a remediation VLAN rather than refused outright.

questions.stem: Sales staff often connect their laptops to hotel and café Wi-Fi without using the VPN. Which control MOST directly protects the laptops from other devices on those networks?
options: The intrusion detection system at head office
A host-based firewall enforced on each device
The perimeter firewall at the main data centre
A web application firewall for the company portal
rationales: Head office IDS never sees traffic on a hotel network.
Correct. A host firewall travels with the device and blocks unsolicited connections wherever it is.
The perimeter firewall protects the corporate network, not laptops outside it.
A WAF protects the portal, not the laptops.
questions.concept: Controls must travel with mobile endpoints.
questions.trap: Relying on network controls the device is not behind.
questions.managerLens: Assume laptops live on hostile networks; protect them on the device.
questions.practicalNote: Always-on VPN or ZTNA clients plus host firewalls and EDR are the usual endpoint baseline.
questions.gap: Protecting endpoints off the corporate network.

questions.stem: Finance wants to stop paying for vendor support on the core switches to save money, arguing that the hardware rarely fails. What is the MOST important security reason to keep support?
options: Support contracts include free training for network engineers
Vendors provide new features only to customers under contract
Support lets engineers raise tickets about performance tuning
Firmware fixes for vulnerabilities and fast replacement parts
rationales: Training is a benefit but not the security reason.
New features are not the security concern.
Performance help is useful but secondary.
Correct. Without support, firmware security fixes and replacement hardware may not be available, leaving known vulnerabilities and long outages.
questions.concept: Supportability is a security property of infrastructure.
questions.trap: Thinking of support only as hardware repair.
questions.managerLens: Present the risk of losing fixes to the business owner who decides on the saving.
questions.practicalNote: Some vendors release security fixes only to customers with active support.
questions.gap: Valuing vendor support in security terms.

questions.stem: A company wants to block an unapproved file-sharing application that runs over TCP port 443, while allowing ordinary HTTPS browsing on the same port. Which firewall capability is needed?
options: Application awareness in a next-generation firewall
A stateful firewall rule that blocks TCP port 443
A packet filter rule that blocks the app's server address
Network address translation on the internet firewall
rationales: Correct. NGFWs identify applications by behaviour and signatures, so they can block one application on port 443 and allow others.
Blocking port 443 would stop all HTTPS browsing.
Such services use many changing addresses, so address rules are easy to evade.
NAT translates addresses; it does not identify applications.
questions.concept: Port-based rules cannot tell applications apart on shared ports; NGFWs can.
questions.trap: Thinking in ports when the requirement is about applications.
questions.managerLens: Write policy in terms of applications and users, not ports.
questions.practicalNote: Application identification often needs TLS inspection, which brings privacy and certificate trust decisions.

questions.stem: Remote staff use a VPN with split tunnelling: corporate traffic goes through the tunnel, while everything else goes straight to the internet from their homes. What is the MAIN security risk of this design?
options: The VPN concentrator must handle every user's internet traffic
Internet traffic bypasses the company's web filtering and inspection
Corporate traffic inside the tunnel is no longer encrypted
Users cannot reach cloud applications while they are connected
rationales: That describes full tunnelling, which split tunnelling avoids.
Correct. With split tunnelling, browsing and downloads skip corporate controls, and a compromised laptop can act as a bridge between the internet and the corporate network.
Traffic in the tunnel is still encrypted.
Users reach cloud applications directly; that is a reason split tunnelling is used.
questions.concept: Split tunnelling trades control for performance.
questions.trap: Confusing split and full tunnelling.
questions.managerLens: Decide by risk; compensate with endpoint controls or cloud-delivered security if split tunnelling is kept.
questions.practicalNote: Secure web gateways delivered from the cloud can inspect traffic that does not go through the VPN.

questions.stem: A payroll software vendor needs to support its application on a company server a few times a year. The vendor asks for a standing VPN account. What is the BEST way to provide access?
options: Give the vendor a standing VPN account with access to the server subnet
Share a company administrator's account with the vendor when it calls
Approve access per request through a jump host with MFA and session recording
Install a remote-control tool on the server that the vendor can use at any time
rationales: A standing account with subnet access is a permanent, broad entry point used a few times a year.
Shared accounts destroy accountability and reveal internal credentials.
Correct. Access that is approved when needed, narrowly scoped, authenticated with MFA and recorded gives the vendor what it needs and nothing more.
Always-available remote control tools are a favourite entry point for attackers.
questions.concept: Third-party access is just-in-time, least-privilege and monitored.
questions.trap: Granting convenient standing access.
questions.managerLens: Put access terms in the contract and enforce them technically.
questions.practicalNote: Privileged access management tools broker and record vendor sessions without revealing passwords.

questions.stem: An outsider joined a company's board video meeting using a meeting link that had been forwarded by email. Which control BEST prevents this happening again?
options: A waiting room where the host admits expected attendees
Telling attendees to keep their cameras switched off
Recording meetings automatically for later review
Using the same meeting link for each board meeting
rationales: Correct. A lobby or waiting room means a forwarded link alone is not enough; the host decides who joins.
Cameras off does nothing to stop an outsider listening.
Recording helps investigation but does not stop the intrusion.
Reusing one link for every meeting makes it more likely to leak and be used by outsiders.
questions.concept: Meeting controls: unique links, passcodes and host-controlled admission.
questions.trap: Choosing a detective control for a preventive need.
questions.managerLens: Set secure defaults for sensitive meetings so hosts do not have to remember.
questions.practicalNote: Authenticated-only meetings, which require attendees to sign in, are common for board sessions.

questions.stem: A company is making remote working permanent for 600 staff who use company laptops at home. Which TWO controls BEST protect access to corporate applications? (Select TWO.)
options: Always-on VPN or zero trust network access with device posture checks
Multi-factor authentication for access to corporate applications
Asking staff to hide their home Wi-Fi network names
Requiring staff to use WEP encryption on their home routers
Letting staff use personal laptops if the company laptop is slow
rationales: Correct. Brokered, encrypted access that checks the device keeps corporate applications off the open internet and away from unhealthy devices.
Correct. MFA protects against stolen passwords, the most common way in.
Hidden network names are easily discovered and add no real protection.
WEP encryption is broken and can be cracked in minutes; it should never be used.
Unmanaged personal laptops undo device controls.
questions.concept: Remote access security rests on brokered access, device health and strong authentication.
questions.trap: Trying to secure home networks the company does not control.
questions.managerLens: Secure what you control: identity, device and access path.
questions.practicalNote: Conditional access can require a compliant device and MFA before any corporate application opens.

questions.stem: A telecom provider manages a bank's branch routers and insists on a permanent management connection into the bank's network. The bank cannot change provider before the contract ends in two years. What should the bank do?
options: Refuse the connection and manage the branch routers internally instead
Accept the connection as requested, since the provider is under contract
Allow it only after the provider passes a one-off penetration test
Limit it to the routers and protocols needed, monitor it, and set terms
rationales: The provider manages the routers under contract; refusing may breach the contract and break the service.
Accepting broad access because of a contract ignores the bank's own duty to control risk.
A one-off test says little about ongoing access and does not limit what the connection can reach.
Correct. Limit the connection to what the service needs, monitor it, and use contract terms on security and notification. That manages the risk within the constraint.
questions.concept: Third-party connections are scoped, monitored and governed by contract.
questions.trap: Choosing an extreme: refuse outright or accept as is.
questions.managerLens: When you cannot remove a risk, constrain and watch it.
questions.practicalNote: Provider connections usually land in a dedicated firewall zone with rules limited to device management protocols.

questions.stem: A hospital wants nurses to see patient records only for patients on the ward they are rostered to, only during their shift, and only from hospital-managed devices. The IAM team already maintains 40 roles and says adding per-ward, per-shift roles is unmanageable. Which access control model fits BEST?
options: Role-based access control with a role for each ward and shift combination
Mandatory access control with labels assigned to each patient record
Discretionary access control with ward managers granting access daily
Attribute-based access control evaluating user, resource and context
rationales: This is the role explosion the IAM team warned about: every ward multiplied by every shift, and RBAC still cannot express the device condition cleanly.
MAC uses classification labels and clearances set centrally. It does not handle dynamic conditions such as roster, time and device.
DAC relies on owners granting access by hand. Daily manual grants are error-prone and do not enforce device or time conditions.
Correct. ABAC evaluates attributes of the subject (role, rostered ward), the resource (the patient's ward) and the context (time, device) in a policy, so one rule covers every ward and shift.
questions.concept: ABAC handles context-dependent decisions without role explosion.
questions.trap: Defaulting to RBAC because it is familiar.
questions.managerLens: Choose the model that enforces the business rule with the least administrative overhead and the fewest errors.
questions.practicalNote: ABAC is often implemented with a policy decision point fed by HR rostering and device-management data.
questions.gap: Not recognising when conditions are attributes rather than roles.

questions.stem: A quarterly access review at a bank finds that a finance analyst who moved to marketing four months ago still holds payment-approval rights in the ERP system. It also finds 30 service accounts with no named owner, several with domain administrator rights. Which TWO process changes address the ROOT causes? (Select TWO.)
options: Trigger access changes from HR mover events, removing previous entitlements
Increase the frequency of user access reviews from quarterly to monthly
Assign a named owner to every service account and include them in reviews
Force service account passwords to change monthly through group policy
Remove the analyst's payment-approval rights in the ERP system immediately
rationales: Correct. The analyst kept old rights because the mover process did not remove them. Driving changes from HR events fixes the cause, not just this case.
More frequent reviews find problems sooner but still rely on catching what the process left behind. It treats the symptom.
Correct. Unowned accounts cannot be reviewed or justified. Ownership is the precondition for reviewing privilege and decommissioning accounts.
Rotation reduces credential exposure but does nothing about missing ownership or excessive privilege.
Necessary today, but it fixes one instance. The question asks for process changes that stop the problem recurring.
questions.concept: Access creep and orphaned accounts come from gaps in the lifecycle process: movers and ownership.
questions.trap: Choosing the immediate fix, or more reviews, instead of the process that caused the finding.
questions.managerLens: Fix the instance and the process; audits find symptoms, management fixes causes.
questions.practicalNote: Link the IAM system to HR as the authoritative source for joiners, movers and leavers, and keep a service account register with owner and purpose.
questions.gap: Not separating corrective action for one case from a root-cause process change.

questions.stem: Staff at a telecom operator have approved fraudulent push notifications after attackers bombarded them with login prompts. Separately, a phishing kit relayed users' passwords and one-time codes to the real portal in real time. Which authentication approach BEST resists both attacks?
options: Push notifications that require users to type a number shown on screen
FIDO2 security keys or passkeys bound to the legitimate site's origin
Time-based one-time passwords generated in an authenticator app
SMS codes with a shorter, 60-second validity period for each login
rationales: Number matching defeats prompt bombing, but an adversary-in-the-middle proxy can show the number to the victim and relay the approval.
Correct. FIDO2/WebAuthn credentials are bound to the site's origin, so a phishing proxy on a different domain cannot obtain a usable assertion, and there is no push to approve.
TOTP codes can be relayed by a real-time phishing proxy within their validity window.
SMS codes can be relayed in real time and are also exposed to SIM swap. A shorter validity does not stop a live relay.
questions.concept: Phishing-resistant MFA: origin-bound public-key credentials (FIDO2/WebAuthn).
questions.trap: Assuming any MFA, or number matching, stops real-time phishing.
questions.managerLens: Roll out phishing-resistant MFA to privileged and high-risk users first, then extend it.
questions.practicalNote: NIST digital identity guidance and CISA treat FIDO2/WebAuthn and PKI-based authenticators as phishing-resistant; OTP and push approval are not.
questions.gap: Not knowing which MFA types resist adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

questions.stem: Chengetedzo's new CISO wants to reduce the risk from the 15 permanent Domain Admin accounts without slowing urgent IT work. Which approach is BEST?
options: Grant admin rights just in time through PAM, approved and recorded
Keep the permanent rights but require the 15 admins to change passwords monthly
Remove admin rights from all but the CIO, who approves every change personally
Rename the Domain Admins group so attackers cannot easily find its members
rationales: Correct. Just-in-time elevation through privileged access management removes standing privilege, keeps a record of who did what, and still lets admins work when needed.
Password rotation does nothing about the 15 always-on targets an attacker can use.
Concentrating approval on one person creates a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
Renaming a group is obscurity; attackers find privileged groups by their identifiers, not names.
questions.concept: Replace standing privilege with just-in-time, approved, recorded elevation.
questions.trap: Tightening the wrong control (passwords) or overcorrecting into a bottleneck.
questions.managerLens: Reduce privileged exposure without stopping the business; measure standing admin accounts.
questions.practicalNote: Tiered administration plus PAM is the usual path to near-zero standing Domain Admins.

questions.stem: Chengetedzo wants to replace the brokers' local accounts with federation to the brokerage's own identity provider. Which TWO statements describe how this should work? (Select TWO.)
options: The brokerage's identity provider authenticates its own staff
The claims portal authorises users from attributes in the assertion
Chengetedzo keeps a local password for every broker as a fallback
The brokerage sends its users' password hashes to Chengetedzo nightly
Chengetedzo's help desk resets brokers' passwords at their request
rationales: Correct. In federation the home organisation's IdP authenticates its own users.
Correct. The portal, as service provider, makes authorisation decisions from the signed assertion's attributes, such as role or broker ID.
Keeping local passwords keeps the old risks and management burden.
Password hashes are never shared in federation; only signed assertions cross the boundary.
Password resets belong to the brokerage's IdP once federation is in place.
questions.concept: Federation: home IdP authenticates; service provider authorises from the assertion.
questions.trap: Keeping local credentials alongside federation.
questions.managerLens: Put deprovisioning duties for partner staff in the federation agreement.
questions.practicalNote: SAML or OpenID Connect are the usual protocols; the agreement covers attributes, assurance and notification of leavers.

questions.stem: An audit at Chengetedzo found 60 building badges still active for people whose network accounts were disabled months ago. What is the BEST fix?
options: Ask facilities to review the badge spreadsheet once each quarter
Install CCTV at entrances to spot former staff who still enter
Drive badge and account changes from one HR-led identity lifecycle
Make the badges expire automatically after twelve months of use
rationales: Quarterly reviews still leave people with access for up to three months and depend on manual checks.
Cameras might detect misuse after the fact; they do not remove access.
Correct. When HR events drive both physical and logical access, a leaver loses both at the same time.
Annual expiry still leaves leavers with access for most of a year.
questions.concept: Converge physical and logical access on one identity lifecycle.
questions.trap: Adding reviews or detection instead of fixing the process.
questions.managerLens: One source of truth for identity means one place to remove access.
questions.practicalNote: Physical access control systems can integrate with HR or identity governance tools to automate badge changes.
questions.gap: Linking physical and logical access management.

questions.stem: An analyst cleared to Secret, working on a border-security project, asks for a Secret report from an unrelated mining-policy project. Her manager says she is trustworthy and senior. Should she get access?
options: Yes, because her clearance matches the report's classification
Yes, because her manager vouches that she is trustworthy
Yes, if she signs a confidentiality agreement for the report
No, unless her current duties require the information
rationales: Clearance is necessary but not enough; it does not establish a need for this report.
Trustworthiness and seniority do not create a need to know.
An agreement adds an obligation but does not justify access.
Correct. Access needs both clearance and need to know; without a duty that requires the report, access is refused.
questions.concept: Need to know limits access even when clearance is sufficient.
questions.trap: Treating clearance as enough on its own.
questions.managerLens: Grant access for a purpose, not for a person's standing.
questions.practicalNote: Compartments and project groups implement need to know in classified environments.
questions.gap: Distinguishing clearance from need to know.

questions.stem: A warehouse uses shared rugged tablets to record stock movements. Workers currently all use one generic login, so nobody can tell who recorded a disputed shipment. What is the BEST approach?
options: Keep the generic login but put a CCTV camera above each tablet station
Have workers tap their badge and enter a short PIN to sign in to a tablet
Give each worker their own tablet so that no device is ever shared
Change the generic password weekly and give it to supervisors only
rationales: Cameras may help reconstruct events but do not create reliable individual accountability in the system.
Correct. Quick individual sign-in (badge plus PIN) keeps shared devices practical while tying every action to a person.
One device per worker solves attribution at large cost and is unnecessary.
A shared password, however often changed, still gives no individual accountability.
questions.concept: Shared devices still need individual authentication for accountability.
questions.trap: Accepting shared accounts because devices are shared.
questions.managerLens: Make the secure option fast enough that workers use it.
questions.practicalNote: Fast user switching with badge tap is common on shared clinical and warehouse devices.

questions.stem: An online banking login asks for a password and then for the answer to a security question about the customer's first school. How many authentication factors does it use?
options: Two factors of different types
Three factors of different types
One factor, used twice
Two factors, both biometric
rationales: Both items are something the user knows, so they are the same factor type.
There are only two items, and both are knowledge.
Correct. A password and a security answer are both 'something you know': single-factor, however many steps.
None of these items is a biometric; both are things the user knows.
questions.concept: Multi-factor means different factor types: know, have, are.
questions.trap: Counting steps instead of factor types.
questions.managerLens: Ask what an attacker needs to steal: two secrets can be phished together.
questions.practicalNote: Security questions are also weak because answers are often guessable or public.

questions.stem: A data centre is choosing between two fingerprint readers. Each vendor quotes one accuracy figure. Which single metric is MOST useful for comparing their overall accuracy?
options: The crossover error rate, where false accepts equal false rejects
The false rejection rate at the vendor's default sensitivity
The time each reader takes to scan and match a fingerprint
The number of fingerprints each reader can store at once
rationales: Correct. The crossover (equal) error rate summarises the trade-off between false accepts and false rejects; lower is more accurate.
FRR alone ignores false acceptances, which can be tuned against it.
Speed is a usability measure, not accuracy.
Capacity says nothing about how accurately the reader matches.
questions.concept: CER (EER) compares biometric accuracy; FAR and FRR trade off against each other.
questions.trap: Comparing one error rate that the vendor can tune.
questions.managerLens: For high-security entry, tune toward low false acceptance and accept some false rejects.
questions.practicalNote: False acceptance is a security failure; false rejection is a usability cost.

questions.stem: A company is updating its password policy to current NIST guidance for staff who also use MFA. Which TWO rules belong in it? (Select TWO.)
options: Check new passwords against lists of known breached passwords
Allow long passphrases and drop rules on mixed character types
Force every user to change their password every 60 days
Require at least one symbol and one capital letter in each password
Let users store password hints that the help desk can read
rationales: Correct. Screening against breached and common passwords blocks the passwords attackers try first.
Correct. Length matters more than complexity, and composition rules push users to predictable patterns.
Forced periodic changes lead to weak, predictable passwords; change only on evidence of compromise.
Composition rules are no longer recommended; they add little strength.
Readable hints give attackers clues and should not be stored.
questions.concept: Modern password guidance: length, breached-password screening, no forced rotation or composition rules.
questions.trap: Following old habits such as 60-day rotation.
questions.managerLens: Spend effort on MFA and breached-password checks, not on rules that annoy users.
questions.practicalNote: NIST SP 800-63B (now Revision 4, 2025) carries this guidance.

questions.stem: A penetration test shows that a cross-site scripting flaw lets attackers read users' session cookies with JavaScript and hijack their sessions. While the flaw is fixed, which cookie setting MOST directly blocks the theft?
options: Extending the session lifetime so users sign in less often
Placing the session identifier in the URL instead of a cookie
Disabling TLS session resumption on the web servers
Setting the HttpOnly flag on the session cookie
rationales: Longer sessions give stolen cookies more time to be useful.
Session IDs in URLs leak through logs, history and referrer headers.
TLS session resumption is unrelated to cookie theft by scripts.
Correct. HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript, so a script injected through XSS cannot steal them.
questions.concept: HttpOnly stops scripts reading session cookies; Secure keeps them on HTTPS.
questions.trap: Choosing a setting that weakens session security.
questions.managerLens: Layer defences: fix the XSS and harden the session.
questions.practicalNote: Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite flags together form the usual session cookie baseline.

questions.stem: A digital bank opens accounts remotely and has been hit by fraudsters using stolen identities. Which TWO measures BEST strengthen its remote identity proofing? (Select TWO.)
options: Verify the ID document and match it to a live selfie with liveness detection
Check the applicant's details against the issuing or authoritative source
Confirm the applicant can receive an email at the address they give
Ask questions drawn from the applicant's public credit history
Send an SMS code to the phone number the applicant provides
rationales: Correct. Document checks plus a liveness-tested biometric match show the person presenting is the person on the document.
Correct. Validating against the issuing authority confirms the identity evidence is genuine and current.
An email address proves only control of that address, which fraudsters create freely.
Knowledge-based questions from credit data are easily answered by fraudsters with stolen data.
An SMS code proves control of a phone number, not identity.
questions.concept: Strong proofing verifies evidence, validates it at source and binds it to the person present.
questions.trap: Confusing proof of contact details with proof of identity.
questions.managerLens: Match proofing strength to the harm a fake account can do.
questions.practicalNote: NIST SP 800-63A defines identity assurance levels (IAL) for proofing strength.
questions.gap: Knowing what makes identity proofing strong.

questions.stem: A company keeps one emergency 'break-glass' administrator account for its cloud tenant. The password is in a sealed envelope in the CIO's safe, and it has not been changed in three years. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Give the password to every IT administrator so it is always available
Disable the account permanently, since it is rarely used
Vault it with logged checkout, alerts on use and rotation after use
Write the password into the IT runbook so the on-call engineer can find it
rationales: Wide sharing destroys control over a highly privileged account.
Without a break-glass account, an identity outage could lock everyone out of the tenant.
Correct. A vault controls and records access, alerts make any use visible, and rotation after use keeps the credential fresh.
Runbooks are widely read; the password would leak.
questions.concept: Emergency accounts are kept, vaulted, monitored and rotated after use.
questions.trap: Either over-sharing or removing the account.
questions.managerLens: Plan for identity failure without creating an unmonitored back door.
questions.practicalNote: Break-glass accounts are usually excluded from conditional access, so monitoring their use is essential.

questions.stem: A bank wants the highest authenticator assurance it can get for its 20 cloud administrators, and is choosing among options that all resist push-fatigue attacks. Which BEST meets the goal?
options: Hardware security keys whose private keys cannot leave the device
Passkeys that synchronise across the administrators' phones and laptops
Authenticator app codes that change every 30 seconds
Push notifications that require typing a number shown on screen
rationales: Correct. Hardware-bound, non-exportable keys are phishing-resistant and meet the highest assurance level, because the secret can never leave the device.
Synced passkeys are phishing-resistant and convenient, but because keys are copied between devices they do not reach the highest level.
One-time codes can be phished and relayed in real time.
Number matching stops push fatigue but not relay through a phishing proxy.
questions.concept: Highest assurance needs phishing-resistant, hardware-bound authenticators.
questions.trap: Assuming all passkeys give the same assurance.
questions.managerLens: Spend the highest assurance where compromise does the most damage: administrators.
questions.practicalNote: NIST SP 800-63B Revision 4 (2025) allows syncable authenticators at AAL2; AAL3 needs non-exportable keys.

questions.stem: In a SAML single sign-on flow between a company's directory and a SaaS expense application, which party issues the signed assertion about the user?
options: The service provider
The user's browser
A directory replica
The identity provider
rationales: The service provider (the expense app) consumes and trusts the assertion.
The browser carries the assertion between parties but does not create it.
A directory replica stores identities; it is not the SAML issuer.
Correct. The identity provider authenticates the user and issues the signed assertion.
questions.concept: IdP issues assertions; SP consumes them.
questions.trap: Confusing the party that carries the assertion with the one that issues it.
questions.managerLens: Protect the IdP's signing keys: whoever holds them can impersonate anyone.
questions.practicalNote: Stolen SAML signing certificates enable forged assertions ('golden SAML').

questions.stem: A mobile app built on REST and JSON needs to sign users in through the company's identity provider and learn who the user is. Which standard is designed for this?
options: OAuth 2.0 access tokens on their own
OpenID Connect with its ID tokens
Kerberos tickets from the domain
LDAP simple bind to the directory
rationales: OAuth 2.0 delegates authorisation to APIs; an access token on its own is not meant to say who the user is.
Correct. OpenID Connect adds authentication to OAuth 2.0: the ID token tells the app who signed in, in a mobile-friendly JSON format.
Kerberos suits internal Windows networks, not mobile apps over the internet.
LDAP simple bind would send credentials to the app and expose the directory; it is not a federation protocol.
questions.concept: OAuth for delegated authorisation; OpenID Connect for authentication on top of it.
questions.trap: Using OAuth access tokens as proof of identity.
questions.managerLens: Standardise on the protocol that fits each app type to avoid home-grown login code.
questions.practicalNote: Mobile apps should use the authorisation code flow with PKCE.

questions.stem: A company synchronises its on-premises Active Directory to a cloud identity provider that controls access to email and 40 SaaS applications. What is the MAIN security implication of this design?
options: Cloud applications can no longer use multi-factor authentication
On-premises users lose single sign-on to internal applications
A compromise of on-premises AD or the sync server reaches the cloud
Password changes must be made separately in each SaaS application
rationales: Hybrid identity does not prevent MFA in the cloud.
Internal SSO continues; synchronisation does not remove it.
Correct. Identities flow from on-premises to the cloud, so an attacker controlling AD or the sync server can create or alter cloud identities. The sync server is a tier-zero asset.
Synchronisation is what lets one password or identity work across services.
questions.concept: In hybrid identity, the on-premises directory and sync path are part of the cloud's trust chain.
questions.trap: Thinking the cloud IdP is isolated from on-premises compromise.
questions.managerLens: Protect sync servers and on-premises identity at the highest tier.
questions.practicalNote: Cloud-only break-glass and admin accounts reduce the blast radius of an on-premises compromise.

questions.stem: On a team file share, the person who creates a document decides who else may read or edit it, and can grant access to colleagues directly. Which access control model is this?
options: Mandatory access control
Role-based access control
Rule-based access control
Discretionary access control
rationales: In MAC the system enforces labels; owners cannot grant access at their discretion.
In RBAC access follows job roles, not individual owners' choices.
Rule-based control applies global rules to everyone.
Correct. Owners deciding who gets access is discretionary access control.
questions.concept: DAC: the owner decides.
questions.trap: Confusing discretion with role-based assignment.
questions.managerLens: DAC is flexible but hard to govern; review owner-granted access regularly.
questions.practicalNote: File system ACLs on Windows and Linux are classic DAC.

questions.stem: A payroll system allows logins only between 06:00 and 19:00 on weekdays and only from the head office network, for every user regardless of role. Which access control model does this describe?
options: Discretionary access control
Rule-based access control
Role-based access control
Mandatory access control
rationales: No owner is deciding access at their discretion.
Correct. Global rules applied to all subjects, such as time and location limits, are rule-based access control.
The rule applies regardless of role, so it is not role-based.
There are no classification labels or clearances.
questions.concept: Rule-based: global rules for everyone.
questions.trap: Confusing rule-based with role-based because of the similar name.
questions.managerLens: Combine models: RBAC for what, rules for when and where.
questions.practicalNote: Conditional access policies often implement rule-based limits such as location.

questions.stem: A user signs in from Harare at 09:00 and, 25 minutes later, from Singapore using the same account. The identity provider blocks the second attempt and asks for stronger authentication. Which kind of access control is at work?
options: Risk-adaptive access control using real-time signals
Discretionary access control set by the account owner
Mandatory access control based on clearance labels
Role-based access control assigned by job function
rationales: Correct. The decision changes with risk signals such as impossible travel: risk-adaptive (risk-based) access control.
The account owner did not set this decision.
No classification labels or clearances play any part in this decision.
The user's role did not change; the context did.
questions.concept: Risk-adaptive access control adjusts decisions to real-time risk.
questions.trap: Thinking access control is fixed once roles are set.
questions.managerLens: Use risk signals to add friction only when risk rises.
questions.practicalNote: Impossible travel, unfamiliar devices and leaked-credential alerts are common risk signals.

questions.stem: A company is building attribute-based access control for its internal APIs, following a zero trust architecture. Which TWO statements about its components are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The policy enforcement point allows or blocks each request at the resource
The policy decision point evaluates policy using attributes and context
The policy enforcement point is where administrators write the policies
The policy decision point must be built separately into each API's code
Only attributes of the user, never of the device, may be considered
rationales: Correct. The PEP sits in front of the resource and enforces the decision it receives.
Correct. The PDP evaluates the request against policy, using attributes of subject, resource and environment.
Policies are authored and administered elsewhere (a policy administration point), not at the PEP.
A central PDP serves many APIs; building one into each API defeats consistency.
ABAC can use device, resource and environment attributes as well as user attributes.
questions.concept: PDP decides; PEP enforces; policies are administered centrally.
questions.trap: Mixing up decision and enforcement.
questions.managerLens: Centralise decisions so policy is consistent; distribute enforcement close to resources.
questions.practicalNote: API gateways often act as PEPs, calling a policy engine as the PDP.

questions.stem: An ERP audit finds that six users hold both the 'create supplier' role and the 'approve payment' role, which together let one person pay a fake supplier. What is the BEST control?
options: Review the six users' transactions once a year for suspicious payments
Raise the payment approval limit so fewer payments need approval
Define a rule in the role model that forbids holding both roles at once
Ask the six users to sign a declaration that they will not misuse access
rationales: Annual review might detect fraud long after it happens; it does not prevent it.
Changing limits does nothing about the conflicting roles.
Correct. A separation-of-duties rule in the role model prevents the toxic combination from being assigned at all.
A declaration is a weak deterrent, not a control on the conflict.
questions.concept: Enforce separation of duties by preventing conflicting role combinations.
questions.trap: Choosing detection or declarations over prevention.
questions.managerLens: Define toxic combinations with the business, then enforce them in the IAM system.
questions.practicalNote: Identity governance tools flag and block SoD conflicts at request time.

questions.stem: A company runs a quarterly review of who can access its customer database. Who should confirm whether each person's access is still needed?
options: The database administrators, who manage the accounts
The service desk, which created the accounts originally
The security team, which owns the access review process
Managers and the data owner, who know the business need
rationales: DBAs know the technical accounts but not whether each person still needs access.
The service desk executes requests; it cannot judge business need.
Security runs the process and checks quality, but should not certify the need itself.
Correct. People who know the work and own the data are best placed to confirm or remove access.
questions.concept: Access reviews are certified by managers and data owners.
questions.trap: Leaving certification to IT or security.
questions.managerLens: Make the business accountable for who can see its data.
questions.practicalNote: Rubber-stamping is common; sample certifications and challenge reviewers who approve everything.

questions.stem: A senior administrator is leaving next week. He is the recorded owner of 12 service accounts and the only person who knows their passwords. What must happen before he leaves?
options: Disable the 12 service accounts on his last day as part of offboarding
Assign new owners and rotate every credential he knew, then offboard
Ask him to write the passwords down and hand them to his manager
Leave the accounts unchanged, since they run systems that are stable
rationales: Disabling running service accounts would break the systems that depend on them.
Correct. Accounts need accountable owners, and any credential a leaver knew must be changed. Ideally they move to managed or vaulted credentials.
Writing passwords down spreads knowledge of them and leaves them unchanged after he goes.
Unchanged credentials known to a former employee remain a standing risk.
questions.concept: Leavers' knowledge of shared or service credentials must be neutralised by rotation.
questions.trap: Thinking that removing the leaver's own account is enough.
questions.managerLens: Make service account ownership and rotation part of the leaver checklist.
questions.practicalNote: Group managed service accounts rotate passwords automatically, so nobody needs to know them.

questions.stem: A directory review finds 40 user accounts that nobody has signed in to for over 120 days. Policy says inactive accounts should be disabled after 90 days. What should happen?
options: Disable them, confirm with managers, and delete those not needed
Delete them all straight away, since the policy has been breached
Leave them, since inactive accounts cannot be used by anyone
Reset their passwords to a random value and keep them enabled
rationales: Correct. Disabling removes the risk at once while managers confirm whether any are still needed, such as staff on long leave.
Immediate deletion can destroy data and break legitimate cases such as extended leave.
Dormant accounts are prime targets: their misuse goes unnoticed.
Enabled accounts remain usable if the new password is reset by an attacker or a help desk mistake.
questions.concept: Dormant accounts are disabled first, then reviewed and removed.
questions.trap: Either ignoring them or deleting without checking.
questions.managerLens: Automate inactivity disabling; investigate any sign-in to a dormant account.
questions.practicalNote: In AD, Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive finds them; schedule it and alert.

questions.stem: A company is cleaning up 300 service accounts in Active Directory. Which TWO practices should its new standard require? (Select TWO.)
options: Use managed service accounts whose passwords the platform rotates
Deny interactive and remote desktop sign-in for service accounts
Share one service account across applications to reduce the count
Give service accounts Domain Admin rights to avoid permission errors
Set service account passwords to never expire so services keep running
rationales: Correct. Managed service accounts rotate long random passwords automatically, so no person knows them.
Correct. Service accounts should run services, not be used by people; blocking interactive logon limits misuse.
Sharing accounts widens the blast radius and destroys accountability.
Excessive rights turn any service compromise into a domain compromise.
Non-expiring, manually set passwords tend to be weak, widely known and never changed.
questions.concept: Service accounts: owned, least privilege, managed credentials, no interactive use.
questions.trap: Optimising for fewer outages at the cost of privilege.
questions.managerLens: Treat service accounts as identities with owners and reviews, not as plumbing.
questions.practicalNote: Kerberoasting targets service accounts with weak passwords and SPNs; managed accounts defeat it.

questions.stem: A user signed in to a Windows domain this morning and received a TGT. She now opens a file share. Which Kerberos component issues the ticket she needs for the file share?
options: The file server itself
The authentication service
The ticket-granting service
The user's workstation
rationales: The file server validates the service ticket but does not issue it.
The authentication service issued the TGT at sign-in.
Correct. The ticket-granting service accepts the TGT and issues a service ticket for the file share.
The workstation requests tickets; it does not issue them.
questions.concept: Kerberos: AS issues the TGT; TGS issues service tickets.
questions.trap: Mixing up the two KDC services.
questions.managerLens: The KDC is tier-zero: protect domain controllers above everything else.
questions.practicalNote: In Active Directory, both services run on every domain controller.

questions.stem: After a virtual machine migration, users at one branch can no longer sign in to the domain. The branch server's clock is nine minutes ahead of the domain controllers. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The branch firewall is blocking LDAP queries
Kerberos rejects tickets outside the clock skew
The users' passwords expired during the migration
DNS records for the branch server were deleted
rationales: Blocked LDAP would cause other errors and does not match the clock evidence.
Correct. Kerberos relies on timestamps; by default clocks may differ by no more than five minutes, so authentication fails.
Password expiry would not depend on the server's clock in this way.
Deleted DNS records cause name resolution errors, not this pattern.
questions.concept: Kerberos needs synchronised time.
questions.trap: Chasing network causes when the evidence points to time.
questions.managerLens: Time synchronisation is a security dependency; monitor it.
questions.practicalNote: Domain members should sync from the domain hierarchy, with the root DC syncing from a reliable source.

questions.stem: A telecom wants central authentication for engineers who log in to routers and switches, with approval of individual commands and full encryption of the AAA traffic. Which protocol fits BEST?
options: TACACS+ over TCP
RADIUS over UDP
LDAP simple bind
Kerberos tickets
rationales: Correct. TACACS+ separates authentication, authorisation and accounting, supports per-command authorisation and encrypts the whole payload.
RADIUS combines authentication and authorisation and encrypts only the password field.
LDAP simple bind is a directory operation, not a device AAA protocol, and sends credentials in clear without TLS.
Kerberos is not used for per-command authorisation on network devices.
questions.concept: TACACS+ for device administration; RADIUS for network access.
questions.trap: Choosing RADIUS because it is the more familiar AAA protocol.
questions.managerLens: Record every privileged command on core devices.
questions.practicalNote: Many networks use TACACS+ for device admin and RADIUS for Wi-Fi and VPN user access.

questions.stem: A security review of a company's Active Directory finds weak authentication settings. Which TWO changes BEST protect directory authentication? (Select TWO.)
options: Require LDAP signing and channel binding, or LDAPS, for directory binds
Disable LM and NTLMv1 authentication across the domain
Allow anonymous directory binds so applications can query users
Store user passwords with reversible encryption for help desk recovery
Extend Kerberos ticket lifetimes to 30 days to cut authentication prompts
rationales: Correct. Signing, channel binding or TLS protect binds from interception and relay attacks.
Correct. LM and NTLMv1 are weak and easily cracked or relayed; removing them closes known attacks.
Anonymous binds expose directory data to anyone on the network.
Reversible encryption is close to storing passwords in clear text.
Long ticket lifetimes extend the value of stolen tickets.
questions.concept: Harden directory authentication: protected binds, no legacy protocols.
questions.trap: Trading security for convenience in directory settings.
questions.managerLens: Treat Active Directory as tier-zero with a hardening baseline and regular assessment.
questions.practicalNote: Free AD assessment tools report these settings and many more.

questions.stem: The board asks whether an outsider on the guest Wi-Fi could actually reach payroll data. The firewall team says the rules prevent it, and last month's vulnerability scan found no critical issues on the payroll servers. Which assessment would answer the board's question MOST directly?
options: An authenticated vulnerability scan of the payroll servers and databases
A line-by-line review of the firewall rule base by an independent auditor
A penetration test from the attacker's starting point, with agreed rules
A configuration audit of the payroll servers against CIS benchmarks
rationales: A scan lists known weaknesses on the targets. It does not show whether they can be reached and exploited from the guest network.
A rule review checks the intended policy, not actual reachability through misconfigurations, other paths or chained weaknesses.
Correct. Only a test that starts where the attacker would start and tries to reach the data shows whether it is actually possible.
Hardening audits check settings against a baseline. Useful, but they do not test the attack path the board asked about.
questions.concept: Penetration testing demonstrates exploitability; scanning finds candidate weaknesses.
questions.trap: Treating a clean scan or a reviewed rule base as proof that no attack path exists.
questions.managerLens: Match the assessment to the question being asked; the board asked about real-world reachability.
questions.practicalNote: Rules of engagement define scope, timing, contacts and stop conditions, and are signed by someone with authority over the systems.
questions.gap: Not distinguishing what scans, audits and penetration tests each prove.

questions.stem: A penetration test finds a critical SQL injection flaw in the customer portal. The product owner wants to defer the code fix to the next release in five months, saying the web application firewall already blocks the test payloads. Security operations confirms the WAF rule is in blocking mode. What should the security manager do?
options: Route a time-limited exception to the accountable executive; test the WAF rule.
Require the portal to go offline until developers deploy and verify the code fix for the flaw.
Downgrade the finding's severity in the report, because a compensating control is now in place.
Accept the product owner's plan and ask the testers to confirm the fix after the next release.
rationales: Correct. A risk this size needs a formal exception: approved by the person accountable for the business risk, time-limited, and conditional on a compensating control proven to work. WAF rules for SQL injection are often bypassable, so test them.

Taking a revenue-generating portal offline may be justified under active exploitation, but doing it without assessing the compensating control is disproportionate and is not the security manager's call alone.
The flaw still exists in the code. A compensating control changes the residual risk recorded in the risk register, not the technical severity of the finding.
A product owner may lack the authority to accept a critical risk, and nobody has checked that the WAF stops variants. This skips exception handling.
questions.concept: Exception handling: documented, approved by the accountable owner, time-bound, with verified compensating controls.
questions.trap: Treating a compensating control as a fix, or jumping to the most disruptive option.
questions.managerLens: Neither block the business nor rubber-stamp: put the decision with the right authority, with evidence and an expiry date.
questions.practicalNote: Track exceptions in the risk register with an owner and expiry, and retest the WAF rule with encoding and evasion variants.
questions.gap: Not knowing how findings move from report to remediation or to a formal exception.

questions.stem: The board of Zambezi Pay wants confidence that internal audit's findings on IT controls are objective. What change matters MOST?
options: Double the size of the internal audit team so it covers more systems
Have the penetration testing firm review internal audit's reports
Have internal audit report to the board's audit committee instead
Ask the CFO to sign off each audit report before it reaches the board
rationales: More auditors increase coverage but not independence; they still report to the person who owns IT.
A test firm reviewing audit reports does not fix the reporting line and is outside its role.
Correct. Auditors reporting to the CFO, who owns IT, are auditing their own boss's area. A direct line to the audit committee protects their objectivity.
CFO sign-off would deepen the conflict, letting the owner of IT filter findings about IT.
questions.concept: Internal audit independence depends on reporting to the board or audit committee.
questions.trap: Fixing capacity when the problem is independence.
questions.managerLens: Assurance is only as good as the independence of whoever gives it.
questions.practicalNote: The audit committee usually approves the internal audit charter and plan, and meets the head of audit privately.

questions.stem: Zambezi Pay's merchant clients want independent assurance that its security controls operated effectively across the year. Which TWO should Zambezi Pay provide? (Select TWO.)
options: A SOC 2 Type II report from an independent auditor covering twelve months
A bridge letter covering the gap between the report period and the request
A SOC 1 report on controls relevant to the merchants' financial reporting
Internal audit's own assessment, signed by the head of internal audit
The executive summary of the latest annual penetration test
rationales: Correct. A SOC 2 Type II report tests whether security controls operated effectively over a period, by an independent auditor.
Correct. A bridge letter states that nothing material has changed since the report period ended, covering the gap until the next report.
SOC 1 addresses controls over financial reporting, not the security assurance the clients asked for.
Internal audit is not independent of the company the clients are assessing.
A penetration test is a point-in-time technical exercise, not assurance over a year of control operation.
questions.concept: Year-long, independent assurance over security controls is a SOC 2 Type II report, with a bridge letter for the gap.
questions.trap: Choosing SOC 1 or a point-in-time test.
questions.managerLens: Give clients the assurance artefact that answers their question, not the one you happen to have.
questions.practicalNote: Clients usually ask for the report, the bridge letter and the complementary user entity controls they must run themselves.

questions.stem: Zambezi Pay's board dashboard shows 'patches applied this month' in green. Which measure would tell the board MORE about vulnerability risk?
options: The total number of vulnerability scans run during the month
The share of critical vulnerabilities fixed within the agreed time
The number of patch tickets closed by each system administrator
The number of systems registered in the patching tool
rationales: Counting scans measures activity, not whether risk went down.
Correct. Remediation of critical vulnerabilities within an agreed time is an outcome measure linked to risk.
Tickets per administrator measures workload, not exposure.
Tool coverage is useful context but says nothing about whether critical issues are fixed.
questions.concept: Prefer outcome metrics tied to risk over activity counts.
questions.trap: Accepting a green activity metric as evidence of security.
questions.managerLens: Report what the board can act on: exposure, trend and exceptions.
questions.practicalNote: Pair the metric with the number of overdue critical items on important systems, named by owner.

questions.subtopic: Choosing internal, external or third-party assessment
questions.stem: A banking regulator requires a bank to obtain an independent opinion on its information security controls each year, to be submitted directly to the regulator. Which kind of assessment meets this requirement?
options: An internal audit by the bank's own audit function
A self-assessment completed by the security team
A third-party assessment of the bank's suppliers
An external audit by an independent outside firm
rationales: Internal audit is independent of management but not of the bank itself, which the regulator asked for.
A self-assessment by the team that runs the controls is not independent at all.
Third-party assessments look at suppliers, not the bank's own controls.
Correct. An external audit by an outside firm gives the independent opinion the regulator requires.
questions.concept: Internal, external and third-party assessments serve different purposes.
questions.trap: Treating internal audit as independent enough for an external requirement.
questions.managerLens: Choose the assessment type that the recipient of the assurance will accept.
questions.practicalNote: Regulators often specify the qualifications or accreditation of external assessors.

questions.stem: A company plans a penetration test of its applications running on a public cloud platform. Which TWO conditions must the test plan meet? (Select TWO.)
options: Follow the cloud provider's published testing policy and permission rules
Limit the scope to the company's own tenant resources and applications
Include attempts to break out of the cloud provider's hypervisor isolation
Include a full-scale denial-of-service test of the cloud provider's network
Avoid telling anyone at the company so the test stays realistic
rationales: Correct. Providers set rules on what customers may test and sometimes require notice; ignoring them can breach the contract.
Correct. Customers may test what they own; shared provider infrastructure is out of scope.
Attacking the provider's hypervisor tests infrastructure the company does not own and is not permitted.
Denial-of-service testing against shared infrastructure is usually forbidden and harms other tenants.
Rules of engagement need named contacts who know about the test, so real incidents are not confused with it.
questions.concept: Cloud testing is bounded by the provider's policy and the customer's own resources.
questions.trap: Testing as if the customer owned the whole platform.
questions.managerLens: Get legal and provider terms into the rules of engagement before any test.
questions.practicalNote: Major cloud providers publish penetration testing policies listing permitted and prohibited activities.

questions.stem: A company has budget for deep testing of only some of its 60 applications this year. What should MOST decide which applications get the deepest testing?
options: The order in which the applications were first put into service
Which application teams volunteer for testing first
The risk each carries: its exposure and the data it handles
Spreading the budget evenly so every application gets the same depth
rationales: How long an application has been running says little about how much risk it carries.
Volunteers are not necessarily the riskiest applications.
Correct. Exposure (such as internet-facing) and data sensitivity determine where testing reduces the most risk.
Even spreading wastes depth on low-risk applications and starves high-risk ones.
questions.concept: Assessment depth and frequency follow risk.
questions.trap: Choosing a fair-looking but risk-blind allocation.
questions.managerLens: Defend the testing plan in terms of risk reduced per pound or dollar spent.
questions.practicalNote: A simple tiering (tier 1 internet-facing with sensitive data, tier 2 internal sensitive, tier 3 the rest) is common.

questions.stem: A retailer is agreeing rules of engagement with an external penetration testing firm. Which TWO items MUST the document contain? (Select TWO.)
options: The targets in scope and those explicitly out of scope
Named contacts, stop conditions and sign-off by someone with authority
The exploit code the testers intend to use, attached in full
A guarantee from the testers that systems will suffer no impact
The testers' home addresses and personal phone numbers
rationales: Correct. Clear scope protects both parties and stops testing of systems the retailer cannot authorise.
Correct. Contacts and stop conditions let incidents be handled safely; authorised sign-off makes the test lawful.
Methods are described at a suitable level; attaching exploit code is not required.
No tester can guarantee zero impact; the document manages the risk instead.
Personal details are not needed; business contacts are.
questions.concept: Rules of engagement: scope, timing, contacts, stop conditions and authorised sign-off.
questions.trap: Expecting impossible guarantees instead of managing risk.
questions.managerLens: Never start a test without signed authority; it is what makes the test legal.
questions.practicalNote: Most rules of engagement also set testing windows and how critical findings are reported during the test.
questions.gap: Knowing what rules of engagement contain.

questions.stem: A company's monthly vulnerability scans run without credentials and report few issues on its Windows servers. A consultant suggests giving the scanner a read-only account. What is the MAIN benefit?
options: It sees installed software and patches, so it finds far more
The scans finish faster because fewer network probes are needed
The scanner can fix vulnerabilities automatically once it finds them
The servers no longer need their host-based firewalls during scans
rationales: Correct. Authenticated scans inspect the system from inside: installed versions, missing patches and configuration, which unauthenticated scans largely miss.
Speed may change, but it is not the main benefit.
Scanners report; fixing is done by the system owners through change management.
Host firewalls stay on; the scanner account needs only the access the scan requires.
questions.concept: Authenticated scans give a much fuller picture than unauthenticated ones.
questions.trap: Taking a quiet unauthenticated scan as evidence of good patching.
questions.managerLens: Ask whether scan results come from authenticated scans before trusting them.
questions.practicalNote: Protect scanner credentials: a dedicated, least-privilege account, vaulted and monitored.

questions.stem: A scan reports a critical vulnerability on a payment server. The administrators say they installed the patch last week and ask for the finding to be closed. What should the security analyst do?
options: Close the finding, since the administrators know their own servers
Ignore it until the next monthly scan shows whether it is still there
Escalate to the CISO as an urgent incident before checking anything
Verify the installed version or rescan, and close it only on evidence
rationales: Closing on assurance alone risks leaving a real critical flaw open on a payment server.
Waiting a month leaves a possible critical exposure unresolved.
Escalating as an incident is premature; there is no sign of exploitation yet.
Correct. Findings are closed on evidence: check the version or run a targeted rescan. It may be a false positive, or the patch may not have applied.
questions.concept: Validate findings before closing them; false positives exist, but so do failed patches.
questions.trap: Taking either the scanner or the administrators on trust.
questions.managerLens: Require evidence for closure on critical findings.
questions.practicalNote: Patches sometimes install but need a reboot to take effect, which scanners correctly flag.

questions.stem: A company wants to know how much damage a malicious employee could do with an ordinary staff account and basic knowledge of the network. What kind of penetration test fits?
options: A black box test with no information or account given
A grey box test starting from a standard user account
A white box test with full source code and diagrams
A vulnerability scan of the internet-facing servers
rationales: Black box simulates an outsider with no knowledge, not an insider.
Correct. Grey box gives the testers partial knowledge and access, like an ordinary employee.
White box gives far more knowledge than a typical employee has.
A scan of internet-facing servers does not simulate an insider at all.
questions.concept: Black, grey and white box tests differ in how much the tester knows.
questions.trap: Defaulting to black box as the most realistic option.
questions.managerLens: Match the test's starting point to the threat you are worried about.
questions.practicalNote: Assumed-breach tests start from a compromised workstation to save time on initial access.

questions.stem: After several red team exercises, the SOC still misses the same attack techniques because findings arrive weeks later in a report. Which approach would MOST improve detection?
options: Run red team exercises twice as often as before
Replace the SOC's monitoring platform with a new product
Run purple team exercises with attackers and defenders together
Keep exercises secret from the SOC so its response is more realistic
rationales: More of the same exercise repeats the slow feedback loop.
A new platform does not fix the missing detections or the feedback gap.
Correct. Purple teaming lets defenders see each technique as it runs and tune detections immediately.
Secrecy measures response realistically, but does nothing to close the detection gap.
questions.concept: Purple teams turn attack simulations into immediate detection improvements.
questions.trap: Doing more red teaming when the gap is feedback.
questions.managerLens: Measure exercises by improvements made, not reports produced.
questions.practicalNote: Purple team sessions often walk through techniques from the MITRE ATT&CK framework one at a time.

questions.stem: A bank wants to know within minutes if its online payment journey breaks at night, when real customer traffic is low. Which technique fits BEST?
options: Synthetic transactions run on a schedule against the payment journey
Real user monitoring of customers' sessions in the payment pages
A monthly penetration test of the payment application
A quarterly review of the payment application's server logs
rationales: Correct. Scripted transactions run around the clock and detect failures even when no customers are using the service.
Real user monitoring needs real users; at night there may be none to show the failure.
Penetration tests look for security weaknesses periodically, not functional failures within minutes.
A quarterly log review would find a failure weeks after customers were affected.
questions.concept: Synthetic transactions test functionality proactively; real user monitoring observes actual use.
questions.trap: Choosing passive monitoring when traffic is low.
questions.managerLens: Availability is security too: detect failures before customers do.
