questions.practicalNote: Synthetic checks should use test accounts and be excluded from business reporting.

questions.stem: The test plan for a new expenses application checks that staff can submit and managers can approve claims. A security reviewer asks for tests showing a user cannot approve their own claim. What kind of testing is this?
options: Load testing under peak usage
Regression testing after changes
User acceptance testing by staff
Misuse case testing
rationales: Load testing checks performance under volume.
Regression testing checks that changes have not broken existing features.
Acceptance testing confirms the system does what users need, not what it must refuse.
Correct. Misuse cases describe what a malicious or careless user might try, and test that the system refuses it.
questions.concept: Misuse case testing checks what the system must refuse to do.
questions.trap: Testing only intended functionality.
questions.managerLens: Make misuse cases part of acceptance criteria for sensitive functions.
questions.practicalNote: Self-approval, privilege escalation through URL changes and bypassing limits are classic misuse cases.

questions.stem: A fintech is testing a new REST API that partners will use to initiate payments. Which TWO tests are MOST important for its security? (Select TWO.)
options: Check authorisation on every endpoint, including access to other partners' data
Send malformed, oversized and unexpected input to each parameter
Measure response times under normal partner traffic levels
Check that the API documentation uses consistent formatting
Confirm the API returns data in both JSON and XML formats
rationales: Correct. Broken object-level authorisation, where one partner reaches another's data, is a leading API flaw.
Correct. Fuzzing parameters finds input-handling flaws such as injection and crashes.
Performance testing matters operationally but is not security testing.
Documentation formatting is not a security property.
Supporting extra formats adds attack surface rather than testing it.
questions.concept: Interface testing covers authorisation per object and robust input handling.
questions.trap: Mistaking functional or performance checks for security testing.
questions.managerLens: APIs exposed to partners need security testing before go-live and after each change.
questions.practicalNote: The OWASP API Security Top 10 is a common checklist for API testing.
questions.gap: Knowing what to test in interfaces.

questions.stem: A development team reports that all of its automated security tests pass. A reviewer finds that the tests run only 40% of the code's paths. Which activity revealed this?
options: Load and stress testing
Code coverage analysis
Input fuzz testing
Regression testing
rationales: Load testing measures performance under volume.
Correct. Coverage analysis measures how much of the code the tests actually exercise; passing tests mean little if most code is never run.
Fuzzing feeds unexpected input to find crashes; it does not measure coverage itself.
Regression testing checks for reintroduced defects.
questions.concept: Coverage analysis shows how much of the system testing actually exercises.
questions.trap: Equating passing tests with tested code.
questions.managerLens: Ask for coverage figures alongside test results.
questions.practicalNote: Coverage tools report line, branch and path coverage in CI pipelines.

questions.stem: A company's annual penetration test finds its controls working, but over the following months configuration changes quietly weaken several of them. What would BEST catch such drift between tests?
options: A second annual penetration test six months after the first
A larger, more detailed annual penetration test report
Continuous breach and attack simulation against the key controls
A policy telling administrators not to weaken security settings
rationales: Twice-yearly tests still leave months of undetected drift.
A bigger report on one point in time does not help between tests.
Correct. Breach and attack simulation runs safe attack scenarios continuously and alerts when a control stops blocking or detecting them.
Policy helps but does not detect accidental or unauthorised change.
questions.concept: Continuous control validation catches drift that point-in-time tests miss.
questions.trap: Treating annual tests as continuous assurance.
questions.managerLens: Ask how you would know if a control failed tomorrow.
questions.practicalNote: BAS tools typically test email filtering, endpoint protection, segmentation and data exfiltration paths.

questions.stem: An auditor asks for evidence that a company can recover its ERP data. The IT team offers a report showing that every nightly backup job succeeded for a year. What evidence should the auditor ask for instead?
options: Screenshots of the backup software's dashboard showing green status
The backup schedule and the retention settings for the ERP system
A signed statement from the IT manager that recovery would work
Recent restore test results, with time taken and data checked
rationales: Dashboards show job status, the same thing the report shows.
Configuration shows intent, not recoverability.
A signed statement is an assertion by an interested party, not evidence of recovery.
Correct. Only a test restore, with its duration and a check of the restored data, shows that recovery works.
questions.concept: Backup evidence means restore results, not job success.
questions.trap: Accepting backup activity as proof of recoverability.
questions.managerLens: Ask for evidence that answers the actual question.
questions.practicalNote: Restore tests should include application-level checks, not just files reappearing.

questions.stem: An auditor wants to know whether a company's change approval process actually works, not just whether it exists on paper. Which evidence is BEST?
options: A sample of changes traced to their approved change records
The change management policy, approved by the board last year
The minutes of the change advisory board's last meeting
The number of change requests raised during the year
rationales: Correct. Tracing a sample of actual changes back to approvals tests whether the control operates.
An approved policy shows the control was designed, not that changes actually follow it.
One set of minutes shows the board met, not that every change went through it.
A count says nothing about whether changes were approved.
questions.concept: Test operating effectiveness by sampling real transactions.
questions.trap: Accepting design evidence as proof of operation.
questions.managerLens: Design evidence is necessary; operating evidence is what shows the control works.
questions.practicalNote: Auditors often start from the systems' own change logs, so unrecorded changes are found too.

questions.stem: A CISO is choosing key risk indicators to warn the board early when exposure rises. Which TWO are key risk indicators rather than performance measures? (Select TWO.)
options: Internet-facing systems with critical vulnerabilities older than 30 days
The share of privileged accounts that are not protected by MFA
The number of tickets the service desk closed per analyst
The share of staff who completed this year's awareness course
The average time taken to answer calls to the service desk
rationales: Correct. Old critical vulnerabilities on exposed systems signal rising likelihood of compromise.
Correct. Privileged accounts without MFA are a direct measure of exposure to credential attacks.
Tickets per analyst measures productivity, not risk.
Course completion measures activity in a process.
Call answer time measures service performance.
questions.concept: KRIs signal exposure; KPIs measure process performance.
questions.trap: Using activity or service metrics as risk indicators.
questions.managerLens: Give KRIs thresholds that trigger action when crossed.
questions.practicalNote: Good KRIs have an owner, a threshold and a defined response when they go red.

questions.stem: The board asks for evidence that the company could recover its core banking system within the agreed recovery time. Which evidence is MOST convincing?
options: The disaster recovery plan, reviewed and approved this year
The contract with the provider of the recovery site
Results of the last failover test, with the recovery time achieved
The IT director's assurance that the team is well prepared
rationales: An approved plan shows intent, not capability.
A contract shows a site exists, not that recovery works.
Correct. A test that measured the actual recovery time against the target is direct evidence.
The IT director's assurance is an opinion, not evidence of recovery capability.
questions.concept: Recovery capability is shown by tests that measure results.
questions.trap: Accepting documents as proof of capability.
questions.managerLens: Ask for measured outcomes, not plans.
questions.practicalNote: Record the actual time to recover and any issues found, and track their fixes.

questions.stem: A scan of a company's estate produces 300 findings. One medium-severity flaw on an internet-facing payment server is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. A critical-severity flaw sits on an isolated test server. Which should be fixed FIRST?
options: The critical flaw on the test server, because its CVSS score is higher
The exploited flaw on the payment server, given its exposure and value
Both together, since every finding must be fixed within 30 days
Neither until the full list has been sorted by CVSS score
rationales: CVSS measures technical severity, not the risk in this environment; the isolated test server has little exposure.
Correct. Known exploitation on an exposed, high-value system means the likelihood and impact are both high, so it outranks a higher score on an isolated box.
Uniform deadlines ignore risk and spread effort thinly.
Waiting to sort by severity alone delays fixing the real risk.
questions.concept: Prioritise by risk: exploitation evidence and asset criticality, not severity alone.
questions.trap: Treating CVSS scores as risk rankings.
questions.managerLens: Fix what attackers are actually using on systems that matter first.
questions.practicalNote: Many teams combine CVSS, KEV status, exploit-likelihood scores and asset tiers in their SLAs.

questions.stem: An independent researcher emails a company's general inbox to report a vulnerability in its customer portal and asks how to share details safely. The company has no disclosure policy. What should the company do?
options: Ignore the email, since the researcher was not authorised to test
Threaten legal action so the researcher does not publish anything
Pay the researcher at once to keep the flaw confidential
Acknowledge it, triage and fix it, and publish a disclosure policy
rationales: Ignoring the report leaves the flaw open and may push the researcher to publish.
Threats discourage future reports and invite public disclosure.
Paying for silence without fixing the flaw leaves customers exposed.
Correct. Responsible handling means acknowledging, fixing and coordinating disclosure, and a vulnerability disclosure policy makes future reports safe and routine.
questions.concept: Responsible (coordinated) disclosure and a vulnerability disclosure policy.
questions.trap: Treating the reporter as the threat.
questions.managerLens: Make it easy and safe for outsiders to tell you about flaws.
questions.practicalNote: A security.txt file on the website tells researchers where to report.

questions.stem: A penetration test of a bank's mobile app has finished. The CISO must report the results to the executive committee. Which TWO elements belong in that report? (Select TWO.)
options: A summary of the business risk each serious finding creates
Prioritised remediation actions, each with an owner and a date
The raw output of every tool the testers ran during the test
Working exploit code so executives can see each flaw in action
A full list of the open-source tools the testers used
rationales: Correct. Executives need to understand what each finding means for the business.
Correct. Owned, dated actions make the report actionable and trackable.
Raw tool output belongs in a technical appendix for engineers, not an executive report.
Exploit code is dangerous to circulate and unnecessary for decisions.
Tool lists are technical detail with no decision value for executives.
questions.concept: Executive reports translate findings into business risk and owned actions.
questions.trap: Mistaking technical detail for useful reporting.
questions.managerLens: Write for the decision the reader must make.
questions.practicalNote: Keep the technical detail in an appendix for the teams who will fix the issues.

questions.stem: Internal audit helped design a new privileged access review process last year. The head of audit now proposes that the same auditor audit how well the process operates. What is the BEST response?
options: Assign a different auditor, or an external party, to perform the audit
Allow it, since the auditor understands the process better than anyone
Allow it, provided the auditor's manager reviews the final report
Cancel the audit, since the process was designed by audit and is sound
rationales: Correct. Auditing work you designed is a self-review threat to independence; someone else should do it.
Deep knowledge does not outweigh the conflict of reviewing your own design.
A manager's review reduces but does not remove the self-review problem.
Being designed by audit is no guarantee it works; it still needs independent testing.
questions.concept: Auditors must not audit their own work.
questions.trap: Valuing familiarity over independence.
questions.managerLens: Independence is what makes audit results credible to the board.
questions.practicalNote: Audit standards treat advisory work on a control as a reason to rotate who audits it.

questions.stem: A cloud payroll provider wants a report on its security controls that it can publish on its website for any prospective customer to read. Which report fits?
options: A SOC 1 Type II report
A SOC 2 Type II report
A SOC 3 report
A SOC 1 Type I report
rationales: SOC 1 covers controls relevant to customers' financial reporting and is restricted to specific users.
SOC 2 reports are detailed and normally shared under NDA with customers, not published openly.
Correct. A SOC 3 report is a general-use summary of a SOC 2 examination, designed for public distribution.
SOC 1 Type I is restricted use and covers financial reporting controls at a point in time.
questions.concept: SOC 1: financial reporting; SOC 2: detailed security, restricted; SOC 3: public summary.
questions.trap: Choosing SOC 2 because it covers security, missing the public-use requirement.
questions.managerLens: Use SOC 3 for marketing, SOC 2 for customers' due diligence.
questions.practicalNote: Customers doing real due diligence will still ask for the SOC 2 report itself.
questions.gap: Knowing SOC report types and their audiences.

questions.stem: A hospital outsources its patient-records hosting to a provider outside its control. Which TWO give the hospital the BEST basis for auditing the provider's security? (Select TWO.)
options: A right-to-audit clause in the hosting contract
The provider's independent SOC 2 Type II report
An unannounced penetration test of the provider by the hospital
A security questionnaire filled in by the provider's sales team
Informal conversations with the provider's engineers at conferences
rationales: Correct. Contractual audit rights let the hospital verify controls itself or through an agent.
Correct. An independent report on operating effectiveness gives assurance without a site visit.
Testing a provider's systems without permission may be illegal and breaches the contract.
Sales-completed questionnaires are self-attestation by an interested party.
Informal conversations are not audit evidence.
questions.concept: Third-party audit rests on contractual rights and independent reports.
questions.trap: Choosing informal or unauthorised methods.
questions.managerLens: Write audit rights into contracts before you need them.
questions.practicalNote: Large providers often satisfy audit clauses through shared reports rather than individual visits.

questions.stem: An internal audit finds that quarterly access reviews for the HR system were skipped twice this year. Who should decide how the finding is addressed?
options: The internal auditor, who should then fix the review process directly
Management responsible for the HR system, with audit tracking the action
The external auditor, at the next annual statutory audit
The security team, which should take over HR access reviews
rationales: Auditors who fix what they audit lose their independence.
Correct. Management owns the control and decides the response; audit follows up to confirm the action is completed.
Waiting for the external auditor delays a response management can make now.
Moving the control to security may not be the right fix and is a management decision.
questions.concept: Auditors report; management owns and remediates; audit follows up.
questions.trap: Letting the auditor act as the fixer.
questions.managerLens: Every finding needs a management owner, an action and a date.
questions.practicalNote: Audit committees usually review overdue audit actions at each meeting.

questions.stem: It is 02:45 and encryption is still spreading to other Mutapa servers. What should the incident manager do NEXT?
options: Start restoring the billing servers from last night's copy in Bulawayo.
Phone the CEO for approval before any action that affects service.
Have forensics image every encrypted server before anything changes.
Isolate affected segments and disable the compromised admin accounts.
rationales: Restoring while the attacker still holds domain administrator rights invites re-encryption, and the backups' integrity is not yet known. Recovery follows containment.
The incident response plan should already give the incident manager authority to contain. Waiting for the CEO while encryption spreads increases the damage; inform executives in parallel.
Evidence matters, but imaging every server takes hours while encryption spreads. Contain first, preserving volatile evidence on key systems as part of it.
Correct. The attack is active, so containment comes first: stop the spread and remove the attacker's privileged access, preserving evidence where practical.
questions.concept: Incident response: after detection and confirmation, contain before eradication and recovery.
questions.trap: Rushing to recovery, or letting evidence collection or approvals delay containment.
questions.managerLens: Limit the damage first, under authority delegated in the incident response plan, and keep executives informed in parallel.
questions.practicalNote: Typical ransomware containment: isolate hosts or VLANs at the switch or through EDR, disable compromised accounts, block command-and-control, and protect the backup systems.
questions.gap: Not knowing the order of incident response steps under pressure.

questions.stem: Containment is holding. Before Mutapa relies on its backups to recover billing, which THREE facts from the case MOST undermine confidence that recovery will succeed? (Select THREE.)
options: The last full restore test of the billing system was 14 months ago.
Backups are copied each night to a second data centre in Bulawayo.
The backup catalogue is held only on the backup server in Harare.
Each backup job is verified with checksums when it completes.
The backup service runs under a domain administrator account.
The billing system gets a full backup each night of the week.
rationales: Correct. An untested restore is an assumption. Fourteen months of change to the billing system means procedures, dependencies and media may no longer work.
Geographic separation is a strength: an event at the Harare site does not destroy the copies.
Correct. If the only catalogue sits on a server in the compromised environment, it may be encrypted, and restores become slow, manual or impossible.
Checksums show the copy matches what was read. That is a strength, though it does not prove the system can be restored.
Correct. The attacker holds domain administrator credentials, so the backups may be deleted, encrypted or tampered with. Backup systems need separate credentials and, ideally, immutable copies.
Nightly full backups support a short recovery point. It is a strength, not a weakness.
questions.concept: Recoverability depends on tested restores, intact backup metadata and backups isolated from production credentials.
questions.trap: Treating successful, verified backup jobs as proof that recovery will work.
questions.managerLens: Ask for evidence of restorability, not of backup activity; fund regular restore tests and isolated, immutable copies.
questions.practicalNote: Ransomware groups routinely target backup consoles with stolen domain administrator credentials; a separate identity domain and immutable storage are now standard advice.
questions.gap: Confusing backup success with recovery capability.

questions.stem: At 23:00 on a Monday, a vendor releases a patch for a remote-access VPN vulnerability that is being actively exploited. The VPN serves 1,200 remote staff, and the vendor rates the patch as low risk to stability. The change advisory board next meets on Thursday. What should happen?
options: Schedule the patch for Thursday's board, since the VPN is critical to the business.
Use the emergency change process: authorised approval now, board review afterwards.
Patch tonight without a change record, because the threat justifies skipping it.
Shut down the VPN until the change advisory board approves the patch on Thursday.
rationales: Waiting three days with an actively exploited flaw on an internet-facing service is an unacceptable exposure.
Correct. Emergency changes still need authorisation from a designated approver, testing proportionate to the urgency, a record, and review at the next board meeting.
Bypassing change management loses the record, rollback planning and accountability, exactly when mistakes during an outage are most likely.
Removing remote access for days has a large business impact and is unnecessary when an emergency route exists. It is a containment option only if patching fails.
questions.concept: Emergency change management: speed with authorisation, documentation and later review.
questions.trap: Thinking urgency means skipping the process, or that following the process means waiting.
questions.managerLens: Good processes have a fast path; use it rather than bypassing or delaying.
questions.practicalNote: An emergency CAB (ECAB) approves out-of-hours changes; many organisations pre-authorise vendor security patches for exposed systems.
questions.gap: Not knowing how change management handles emergencies.

questions.stem: A team builds a Node.js customer app. Its CI pipeline already runs static analysis (SAST) on the team's own code at every commit. Most of the shipped code comes from open-source npm packages. Which TWO additions close the LARGEST remaining testing gaps? (Select TWO.)
options: Software composition analysis of all dependencies in each build
A second static analysis tool from another vendor to cross-check
Dynamic testing against a staging deployment before each release
Code-signing of release artefacts with a key held in an HSM
Linting plug-ins in developers' IDEs to enforce code style
rationales: Correct. SCA inventories open-source dependencies and flags known vulnerabilities and licence issues. SAST on first-party code does not cover them, and they make up most of the app.
Another SAST tool may find a few extra issues, but it tests the same small share of the code in the same way.
Correct. Dynamic testing (DAST) exercises the running application and finds configuration, authentication and runtime issues that static analysis cannot see.
Code signing protects the integrity of what is shipped. Valuable, but it is not testing and finds no vulnerabilities.
Style linting improves consistency. It is not a meaningful security test.
questions.concept: Test coverage: SAST for your own code, SCA for dependencies, DAST for the running app.
questions.trap: Assuming SAST covers third-party components, or confusing integrity controls with testing.
questions.managerLens: Invest where the risk is: most modern code is third-party, so dependency analysis gives the biggest return.
questions.practicalNote: SCA tools also produce SBOMs. DAST usually runs against staging, with authenticated scans for logged-in functions.
questions.gap: Not knowing what each application security testing technique covers.

questions.stem: A ministry is buying a commercial HR system that will hold staff medical and disciplinary records. The vendor refuses to share source code, and its licence forbids reverse engineering. The procurement committee meets next week, and the quoted price expires at month end. Which approach BEST assesses the product's security before purchase?
options: Run a DAST scan against the vendor's public demo instance without asking
Decompile the client application to look for hard-coded secrets and flaws
Require independent test results, an SBOM and security terms in the contract
Rely on the product's market share, since many governments already use it
rationales: Testing a system you do not own without permission may be illegal and breaches the vendor's terms. It also tests a demo, not your deployment.
This breaches the licence agreement and carries legal risk. It is not an approach a manager can approve.

Correct. When you cannot inspect the code, rely on independent assurance (third-party test reports or certifications), transparency about components (an SBOM) and enforceable commitments on vulnerability handling.
Popularity is not assurance. Widely used products are also attractive targets.
questions.concept: Assessing acquired software: independent assurance, transparency and contractual controls.
questions.trap: Testing without authorisation, or substituting popularity for evidence.
questions.managerLens: Make security evidence a procurement requirement, within legal and contractual limits.
questions.practicalNote: Ask for recent independent penetration test summaries, certifications such as Common Criteria where relevant, an SBOM, and a vulnerability disclosure and patching commitment in the contract.
questions.gap: Not knowing the legitimate ways to gain assurance over commercial software.
